section.heading: 15. Multiple Integrals
Introduction

figure.caption: Tumors, such as the one illustrated here, have been modeled as “bumpy spheres.” In Exercise 15.8.49 you are asked to compute the volume enclosed by such a surface.

section.paragraph: IN THIS CHAPTER WE EXTEND the idea of a definite integral to double and triple integrals of functions of two or three variables. These ideas are then used to compute volumes, masses, and centroids of more general regions than we were able to consider in Chapters 6 and 8. We also use double integrals to calculate probabilities when two random variables are involved.

We will see that polar coordinates are useful in computing double integrals over some types of regions. In a similar way, we will introduce two new coordinate systems in three-dimensional space––cylindrical coordinates and spherical coordinates––that greatly simplify the computation of triple integrals over certain commonly occurring solid regions.
section.heading: 15.1. Double Integrals over Rectangles
section.paragraph: In much the same way that our attempt to solve the area problem led to the definition of a definite integral, we now seek to find the volume of a solid and in the process we arrive at the definition of a double integral.
section.heading: Review of the Definite Integral
section.paragraph: First let’s recall the basic facts concerning definite integrals of functions of a single variable. If $$f(x)$$ is defined for $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , we start by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ sub-intervals $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta x = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash n$$ and we choose sample points $$x_{i}^{*}$$ in these subintervals. Then we form the Riemann sum
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f(x_{i}^{*}}){\Delta x}$$
and take the limit of such sums as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ to obtain the definite integral of $$f$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ :
$${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}}}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f{\left( x_{i}^{*} \right)}}{\Delta x}$$

In the special case where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ , the Riemann sum can be interpreted as the sum of the areas of the approximating rectangles in Figure 1, and $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$ represents the area under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ .

section.heading: Volumes and Double Integrals
section.paragraph: In a similar manner we consider a function $$f$$ of two variables defined on a closed rectangle

$$\left. R = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b,c \leqslant y \leqslant d \right. \right\}$$

and we first suppose that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ . The graph of $$f$$ is a surface with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . Let $$S$$ be the solid that lies above $$R$$ and under the graph of $$f$$ , that is,
$$\left. S = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \middle| 0 \leqslant z \leqslant f\left( {x,y} \right),\left( {x,y} \right) \in R \right. \right\}$$
(See Figure 2.) Our goal is to find the volume of $$S$$ .

image.alt: Details A shaded region, a surface, and eight line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. A square shaped region is shaded in the x y plane and labeled R. From the x axis, two line segments from the tick marks a and b, run parallel to the y axis to meet the top and bottom left corners of R, respectively. From the y axis, two line segments from the tick marks c and d, run parallel to the x axis to meet the top left and right corners of R, respectively. A surface, labeled z = f(x, y), is graphed directly above R. It resembles a square that is curved concave up. From each corner of R, a vertical line segment rises upward, parallel to the z axis to meet the respective corners of the surface.

section.paragraph: The first step is to divide the rectangle $$R$$ into subrectangles. We accomplish this by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$m$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta x = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash m$$ and dividing $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {y_{j - 1},y_{j}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta y = \left( {d - c} \right) \slash n$$ . By drawing lines parallel to the coordinate axes through the endpoints of these subintervals, as in Figure 3, we form the subrectangles

$$R_{ij} = \left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {y_{j - 1},y_{j}} \right\rbrack = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x_{i - 1} \leqslant x \leqslant x_{i},y_{j - 1} \leqslant y \leqslant y_{j} \right\}$$
each with area $$\Delta A = \Delta x\Delta y$$ .

image.alt: Details A rectangle divided into smaller rectangles is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The rectangle has short vertical sides and longer horizontal sides. The bottom left and right corners of the rectangle are directly above a and b on the x axis, respectively. The distance between x_(i minus 1) and x_i is labeled Delta x. The first and last line segments meet the bottom left and right corners of the rectangle. The distance between y_(i minus 1) and y_i is labeled Delta y. The first and last line segments meet the bottom and top left corners of the rectangle. The dot within the third cell from the left in the second row from the bottom is labeled (x^*_(3, 2), y^*_(3, 2)).

section.paragraph: If we choose a sample point $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in each $$R_{ij}$$ , then we can approximate the part of $$S$$ that lies above each $$R_{ij}$$ by a thin rectangular box (or “column”) with base $$R_{ij}$$ and height $$f{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}$$ as shown in Figure 4. (Compare with Figure 1.) The volume of this box is the height of the box times the area of the base rectangle:

The height of the line segments is labeled f(x^*_(i j), y^*_(i j)).

section.paragraph: If we follow this procedure for all the rectangles and add the volumes of the corresponding boxes, we get an approximation to the total volume of $$S$$ :
$$V \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f(x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*})}}\Delta A$$
(See Figure 5.) This double sum means that for each subrectangle we evaluate $$f$$ at the chosen point and multiply by the area of the subrectangle, and then we add the results.

image.alt: Details Forty vertical cuboids are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The forty are arranged in eight rows and five columns, without any gaps between them. All of them have a horizontal square base on the x y plane. The cuboid at the back right corner is the tallest and the heights of the other cuboids progressively decrease as we move down the column, across the row and diagonally. The front row cuboids are slightly higher than the previous row. The bottom right corners of the top surfaces of the cuboid appear to be points on a plane curved concave up.

section.paragraph: Our intuition tells us that the approximation given in (3) becomes better as $$m$$ and $$n$$ become larger and so we would expect that
$$V = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f(x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}){\Delta A}}}$$

We use the expression in Equation 4 to define the volume of the solid $$S$$ that lies under the graph of $$f$$ and above the rectangle $$R$$ . (It can be shown that this definition is consistent with our formula for volume in Section 6.2.)

The meaning of the double limit in Equation 4 is that we can make the double sum as close as we like to the number $$V$$ [for any choice of $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in $$R_{ij}$$ ] by taking $$m$$ and $$n$$ sufficiently large.

Limits of the type that appear in Equation 4 occur frequently, not just in finding volumes but in a variety of other situations as well—as we will see in Section 15.4—even when $$f$$ is not a positive function. So we make the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The double integral of $$f$$ over the rectangle $$R$$ is
$${\iint\limits_{R}f}{({x,y})}dA = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f}{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A$$
if this limit exists.
Notice the similarity between Definition 5 and the definition of a single integral in Equation 2.

section.paragraph: The precise meaning of the limit in Definition 5 is that for every number $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there is an integer $$N$$ such that
$$\left| \left. {\iint\limits_{R}f}{({x,y})}dA - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f}{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*})}\Delta A} \middle| \right. < \varepsilon \right.$$
for all integers $$m$$ and $$n$$ greater than $$N$$ and for any choice of sample points $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in $$R_{ij}.$$

Although we have defined the double integral by dividing $$R$$ into equal-sized subrectangles, we could have used subrectangles $$R_{ij}$$ of unequal size. But then we would have to ensure that all of their dimensions approach $$0$$ in the limiting process.

A function $$f$$ is called integrable if the limit in Definition 5 exists. It is shown in courses on advanced calculus that all continuous functions are integrable. In fact, the double integral of $$f$$ exists provided that $$f$$ is “not too discontinuous.” In particular, if $$f$$ is bounded on $$R$$ , [that is, there is a constant $$M$$ such that $$\left| f(x,y) \middle| \leqslant M \right.$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ ], and $$f$$ is continuous there, except possibly on a finite number of smooth curves, then $$f$$ is integrable over $$R$$ .

The sample point $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ can be chosen to be any point in the subrectangle $$R_{ij}$$ , but if we choose it to be the upper right-hand corner of $$R_{ij}$$ [namely $$({x_{i},y_{j}})$$ , see Figure 3], then the expression for the double integral looks simpler:
$${\iint\limits_{R}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f}{({x_{i},y_{i}})}\Delta A$$
By comparing Definitions 4 and 5, we see that a volume can be written as a double integral:
If $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , then the volume $$V$$ of the solid that lies above the rectangle $$R$$ and below the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is
$$V = {\iint\limits_{R}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA$$
The sum in Definition 5,
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f}{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A$$

is called a double Riemann sum and is used as an approximation to the value of the double integral. [Notice how similar it is to the Riemann sum in (1) for a function of a single variable.] If $$f$$ happens to be a positive function, then the double Riemann sum represents the sum of volumes of columns, as in Figure 5, and is an approximation to the volume under the graph of $$f$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Estimate the volume of the solid that lies above the square $$R = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ and below the elliptic paraboloid $$z = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ . Divide $$R$$ into four equal squares and choose the sample point to be the upper right corner of each square $$R_{ij}$$ . Sketch the solid and the approximating rectangular boxes.

Solution The squares are shown in Figure 6. The paraboloid is the graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ and the area of each square is $$\Delta A = 1$$ . Approximating the volume by the Riemann sum with $$m = n = 2$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {V \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{2}f}{\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{V} = f{\left( {1,1} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {1,2} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {2,1} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {2,2} \right)}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{V} = 13(1) + 7(1) + 10(1) + 4(1) = 34} \end{array}$$
This is the volume of the approximating rectangular boxes shown in Figure 7.

section.paragraph: We get better approximations to the volume in Example 1 if we increase the number of squares. Figure 8 shows how the columns start to look more like the actual solid and the corresponding approximations become more accurate when we use $$16$$ , $$64$$ , and $$256$$ squares. In Example 7 we will be able to show that the exact volume is $$48$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: If $$R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1, - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ , evaluate the integral
$${\iint\limits_{R}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dA$$

Solution It would be very difficult to evaluate this integral directly from Definition 5 but, because $$\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \geqslant 0$$ , we can compute the integral by interpreting it as a volume. If $$z = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}$$ , then $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ and $$z \geqslant 0$$ , so the given double integral represents the volume of the solid $$S$$ that lies below the circular cylinder $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ and above the rectangle $$R$$ . (See Figure 9.) The volume of $$S$$ is the area of a semicircle with radius $$1$$ times the length of the cylinder. Thus
$${\iint\limits_{R}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dA = \frac{1}{2}\pi{(1)}^{2} \times 4 = 2\pi$$

It is a semicircle lying on the x z plane, begins from (1, 0, 0), crosses the z axis at (0, 0, 1), and reaches the negative x axis.

section.heading: The Midpoint Rule
section.paragraph: The methods that we used for approximating single integrals (the Midpoint Rule, the Trapezoidal Rule, Simpson’s Rule) all have counterparts for double integrals. Here we consider only the Midpoint Rule for double integrals. This means that we use a double Riemann sum to approximate the double integral, where the sample point $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in $$R_{ij}$$ is chosen to be the center $$({{\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j}})$$ of $$R_{ij}$$ . In other words, $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ is the midpoint of $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ and $${\overline{y}}_{j}$$ is the midpoint of $$\left\lbrack {y_{j - 1},y_{j}} \right\rbrack$$ .

note.title: Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals
note.heading: Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals
note.paragraph: $${\iint\limits_{R}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f}{({{\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j}})}\Delta A$$
where $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ is the midpoint of $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ and $${\overline{y}}_{j}$$ is the midpoint of $$\left\lbrack {y_{j - 1},y_{j}} \right\rbrack$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Use the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 2$$ to estimate the value of the integral $${\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA$$ , where $${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ .

Solution In using the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 2$$ , we evaluate $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x - 3y^{2}$$ at the centers of the four subrectangles shown in Figure 10. So $${\overline{x}}_{1} = \frac{1}{2}$$ , $${\overline{x}}_{2} = \frac{3}{2}$$ , $${\overline{y}}_{1} = \frac{5}{4}$$ , and $${\overline{y}}_{2} = \frac{7}{4}$$ . The area of each subrectangle is $$\Delta A = \frac{1}{2}$$ . Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{2}f}{({{\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j}})}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} = f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{1},{\overline{y}}_{1}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{1},{\overline{y}}_{2}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{2},{\overline{y}}_{1}} \right)}\Delta A + f{({{\overline{x}}_{2},{\overline{y}}_{2}})}\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= f{\left( {\frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{1}{2},\frac{7}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{4}} \right)}\Delta A + f{\left( {\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{4}} \right)}\Delta A}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= \left( {- \frac{67}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{139}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{51}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2} + \left( {- \frac{123}{16}} \right)\frac{1}{2}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA}{= - \frac{95}{8} = - 11.875}} \end{array}$$
Thus we have
$${\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA \approx - 11.875$$

section.paragraph: Note In Example 5 we will see that the exact value of the double integral given in Example 3 is $$- 12$$ . (Remember that the interpretation of a double integral as a volume is valid only when the integrand $$f$$ is a positive function. The integrand in Example 3 is not a positive function, so its integral is not a volume. In Examples 5 and 6 we will discuss how to interpret integrals of functions that are not always positive in terms of volumes.) If we keep dividing each subrectangle in Figure 10 into four smaller ones with similar shape, we get the Midpoint Rule approximations displayed in the table below. Notice how these approximations approach the exact value of the double integral, $$- 12$$ .
section.heading: Iterated Integrals
section.paragraph: Recall that it is usually difficult to evaluate single integrals directly from the definition of an integral, but the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus provides a much easier method. The evaluation of double integrals from first principles is even more difficult, but here we see how to express a double integral as an iterated integral, which can then be evaluated by calculating two single integrals.

Suppose that $$f$$ is a function of two variables that is integrable on the rectangle $$R = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ . We use the notation $$\int_{c}^{d}{f(x,y)dy}$$ to mean that $$x$$ is held fixed and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is integrated with respect to $$y$$ from $$y = c$$ to $$y = d$$ . This procedure is called partial integration with respect to $$y$$ . (Notice its similarity to partial differentiation.) Now $$\int_{c}^{d}{f(x,y)dy}$$ is a number that depends on the value of $$x$$ , so it defines a function of $$x$$ :
$$A(x) = {\int_{c}^{d}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dy$$
If we now integrate the function $$A$$ with respect to $$x$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ , we get
$${\int_{a}^{b}A}(x)dx = {\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack {\int_{c}^{d}{f(x,y)dy}} \right\rbrack}dx$$
The integral on the right side of Equation 7 is called an iterated integral. Usually the brackets are omitted. Thus
$${\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}f}}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dydx = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {{\int_{c}^{d}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dy} \right\rbrack dx}}$$

means that we first integrate with respect to $$y$$ (holding $$x$$ fixed) from $$y = c$$ to $$y = d$$ , and then we integrate the resulting function of $$x$$ with respect to $$x$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ .
Similarly, the iterated integral
$${\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}f}}(x,y)dxdy = {\int_{c}^{d}\left\lbrack {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x,y)dx}} \right\rbrack}dy$$

means that we first integrate with respect to $$x$$ (holding $$y$$ fixed) from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ and then we integrate the resulting function of $$y$$ with respect to $$y$$ from $$y = c$$ to $$y = d$$ . Notice that in both Equations 8 and 9 we work from the inside out.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Evaluate the iterated integrals.
Solution

list.item: (a) Regarding $$x$$ as a constant, we obtain $$\int_{1}^{2}{x^{2}ydy = \left\lbrack x^{2}\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{y = 1}^{y = 2} = x^{2}\left( \frac{2^{2}}{2} \right) - x^{2}\left( \frac{1^{2}}{2} \right) = \frac{3}{2}x^{2}}$$ Thus the function $$A$$ in the preceding discussion is given by $$A(x) = \frac{3}{2}x^{2}$$ in this example. We now integrate this function of $$x$$ from $$0$$ to $$3$$ : $$\int_{0}^{3}\int_{1}^{2}x^{2}ydydx = {\int_{0}^{3}\left\lbrack {\int_{1}^{2}{x^{2}ydy}} \right\rbrack}dx = \int_{0}^{3}\frac{3}{2}x^{2}dx = \frac{x^{3}}{2}\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{27}{2}$$

(b) Here we first integrate with respect to $$x$$ , regarding $$y$$ as a constant: $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydxdy = \int_{1}^{2}\left\lbrack \int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydx \right\rbrack dy = \int_{1}^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{3}}{3}y \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 3}dy} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}x^{2}ydxdy}\left. = {\int_{1}^{2}{9ydy = 9\frac{y^{2}}{2}}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \frac{27}{2}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Notice that in Example 4 we obtained the same answer whether we integrated with respect to $$y$$ or $$x$$ first. In general, it turns out (see Theorem 10) that the two iterated integrals in Equations 8 and 9 are always equal; that is, the order of integration does not matter. (This is similar to Clairaut’s Theorem on the equality of the mixed partial derivatives.)
The following theorem gives a practical method for evaluating a double integral by expressing it as an iterated integral (in either order).

note.title: Fubini’s Theorem
note.heading: Fubini’s Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on the rectangle
$${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b \right.},\left. c \leqslant y \leqslant d \right\}$$
then
$${\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{f(x,y)dydx}}}}} = {\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x,y)dxdy}}}$$
More generally, this is true if we assume that $$f$$ is bounded on $$R$$ , $$f$$ is discontinuous only on a finite number of smooth curves, and the iterated integrals exist.

Theorem 10 is named after the Italian mathematician Guido Fubini (1879–1943), who proved a very general version of this theorem in 1907. But the version for continuous functions was known to the French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy almost a century earlier.

section.paragraph: The proof of Fubini’s Theorem is too difficult to include in this book, but we can at least give an intuitive indication of why it is true for the case where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ . Recall that if $$f$$ is positive, then we can interpret the double integral $${\iint_{R}f({x,y})}dA$$ as the volume $$V$$ of the solid $$S$$ that lies above $$R$$ and under the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . But we have another formula that we used for volume in Section 6.2, namely,

where $$A(x)$$ is the area of a cross-section of $$S$$ in the plane through $$x$$ perpendicular to the $$x$$ -axis. From Figure 11 you can see that $$A(x)$$ is the area under the curve $$C$$ whose equation is $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$x$$ is held constant and $$c \leqslant y \leqslant d$$ . Therefore
$$A(x) = {\int_{c}^{d}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dy$$
and we have
$${\iint\limits_{R}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA = V = {\int_{a}^{b}A}{(x)}dx = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}f}}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dydx$$

$${\iint\limits_{R}f}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA = {\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}f}}{\left( {x,y} \right)}dxdy$$

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Evaluate the double integral $${\iint_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA$$ , where $${R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2 \right.},\left. 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2 \right\}$$ . (Compare with Example 3.)
Solution 1 Fubini’s Theorem gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{1}^{2}{(x - 3y^{2})}}}dydx = {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {xy - y^{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 1}^{y = 2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})}}dA} = \left. {\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {x - 7} \right)}}dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 7x \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = - 12} \end{array}$$
Solution 2 Again applying Fubini’s Theorem, but this time integrating with respect to $$x$$ first, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})dA = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{2}{(x - 3y^{2})dxdy}}}}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - 3xy^{2}} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 2}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{(x - 3y^{2})dA}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{(2 - 6y^{2})dy = \left. {2y - 2y^{3}} \right\rbrack}}_{1}^{2} = - 12} \end{array}$$

Notice the negative answer in Example 5; nothing is wrong with that. The function f is not a positive function, so its integral doesn’t represent a volume. From Figure 13 we see that $$f$$ is always negative on $$R$$ , so the value of the integral is the negative of the volume that lies above the graph of $$f$$ and below $$R$$ .

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\iint_{R}y}\sin{\left( {xy} \right)}dA$$ , where $$R = \left\lbrack {1,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack$$ .
Solution If we first integrate with respect to $$x$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{1}^{2}{y\sin(xy)dxdy}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}} = {{\int_{0}^{\pi}{y\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{y}\cos(xy)} \right\rbrack_{x = 1}^{x = 2}}}dy}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}}{= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{( - \cos 2y + \cos y)dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{y\sin(xy)dA}}{= - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2y + \sin y\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = 0}} \end{array}$$

For a function $$f$$ that takes on both positive and negative values, $$\iint_{R}{f(x,y)dA}$$ is a difference of volumes: $$V_{1} - V_{2}$$ , where $$V_{1}$$ is the volume above $$R$$ and below the graph of $$f$$ , and $$V_{2}$$ is the volume below $$R$$ and above the graph. The fact that the integral in Example 6 is $$0$$ means that these two volumes $$V_{1}$$ and $$V_{2}$$ are equal. (See Figure 14.)

section.paragraph: Note In Example 6, if we reverse the order of integration and first integrate with respect to $$y$$ , we get
$${\iint\limits_{R}y}\sin{\left( {xy} \right)}dA = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi}y}}\sin{\left( {xy} \right)}dydx$$

but this order of integration is much more difficult than the method given in the example because it involves integration by parts twice. Therefore, when we evaluate double integrals it is wise to choose the order of integration that gives simpler integrals.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid $$S$$ that is bounded by the elliptic paraboloid $$x^{2} + 2y^{2} + z = 16$$ , the planes $$x = 2$$ and $$y = 2$$ , and the three coordinate planes.

Solution We first observe that $$S$$ is the solid that lies under the surface $$z = 16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}$$ and above the square $$R = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ . (See Figure 15.) This solid was considered in Example 1, but we are now in a position to evaluate the double integral using Fubini’s Theorem. Therefore

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{R}{({16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}})}dA = \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{2}{({16 - x^{2} - 2y^{2}})}dxdy} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {16x - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - 2y^{2}x} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 2}dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{{\left( {\frac{88}{3} - 4y^{2}} \right)}dy = \left\lbrack {\frac{88}{3}y - \frac{4}{3}y^{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = 48}}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: In the special case where $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ can be factored as the product of a function of $$x$$ only and a function of $$y$$ only, the double integral of $$f$$ can be written in a particularly simple form. To be specific, suppose that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = g(x)h(y)$$ and $$R = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ . Then Fubini’s Theorem gives
$${\iint\limits_{R}{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA =}}{\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)h{(y)}dxdy =}}}{\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)h(y)dx}} \right\rbrack dy}}$$
In the inner integral, $$y$$ is a constant, so $$h(y)$$ is a constant and we can write

$${{\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)h{(y)}dx}} \right\rbrack dy =}}{\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {h(y)\left( {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}} \right)} \right\rbrack dy}}}{= {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}}{\int_{c}^{d}{h{(y)}dy}}}$$
since $$\int_{a}^{b}{g{(x)}dx}$$ is a constant. Therefore, in this case the double integral of $$f$$ can be written as the product of two single integrals:
$${\iint\limits_{R}{g(x)h{(y)}dA}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{g{(x)}dx}}\int_{c}^{d}h(y)dy$$
where
$$R = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: if $$R = \left\lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,\pi \slash 2\rbrack \right.$$ , then, by Equation 11,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}{\sin x\cos ydA = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sin xdx{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\cos ydy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}{\sin x\cos ydA}}{= \left\lbrack - \cos x \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack \sin y \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1}} \end{array}$$
The function $$f(x,y) = \sin x\cos y$$ in Example 8 is positive on $$R$$ , so the integral represents the volume of the solid that lies above $$R$$ and below the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 16.

section.heading: Average Value
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 6.5 that the average value of a function $$f$$ of one variable defined on an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is
In a similar fashion we define the average value of a function $$f$$ of two variables defined on a rectangle $$R$$ to be
$$f_{avg} = \frac{1}{A(R)}{\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA}}$$
where $$A(R)$$ is the area of $$R$$ .
If $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , the equation
$$A(R) \times f_{avg} = {\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA}}$$

says that the box with base $$R$$ and height $$f_{avg}$$ has the same volume as the solid that lies under the graph of $$f$$ . [If $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ describes a mountainous region and you chop off the tops of the mountains at height $$f_{avg}$$ , then you can use them to fill in the valleys so that the region becomes completely flat. See Figure 17.]

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: The contour map in Figure 18 shows the snowfall, in inches, that fell on the state of Colorado on December 20 and 21, 2006. (The state is in the shape of a rectangle that measures $$388$$ mi west to east and $$276$$ mi south to north.) Use the contour map to estimate the average snowfall for the entire state of Colorado on those days.

example.paragraph: Solution Let’s place the origin at the southwest corner of the state. Then $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 388$$ , $$0 \leqslant y \leqslant 276$$ , and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is the snowfall, in inches, at a location $$x$$ miles to the east and $$y$$ miles to the north of the origin. If $$R$$ is the rectangle that represents Colorado, then the average snowfall for the state on December 20–21 was
$$f_{avg} = \frac{1}{A(R)}{\iint\limits_{R}{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA}}$$

where $$A(R) = 388 \cdot 276$$ . To estimate the value of this double integral, let’s use the Midpoint Rule with $$m = n = 4$$ . In other words, we divide $$R$$ into $$16$$ subrectangles of equal size, as in Figure 19. The area of each subrectangle is

example.paragraph: Using the contour map to estimate the value of $$f$$ at the center of each subrectangle, we get

$$\begin{matrix} {\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{4}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{4}f({\overline{x}}_{i},{\overline{y}}_{j})\Delta A} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} \approx {\Delta A}\lbrack 0 + 15 + 8 + 7 + 2 + 25 + 18.5 + 11 +} \\ { 4.5 + 28 + 17 + 13.5 + 12 + 15 + 17.5 + 13\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} = (6693)(207)} \end{matrix}$$
Therefore
On December 20–21, 2006, Colorado received an average of approximately $$13$$ inches of snow.

section.heading: 15.2. Double Integrals over General Regions
section.paragraph: For single integrals, the region over which we integrate is always an interval. But for double integrals, we want to be able to integrate a function not just over rectangles but also over regions of more general shape.
section.heading: General Regions
section.paragraph: Consider a general region $$D$$ like the one illustrated in Figure 1. We suppose that $$D$$ is a bounded region, which means that $$D$$ can be enclosed in a rectangular region $$R$$ as in Figure 2. In order to integrate a function $$f$$ over $$D$$ we define a new function $$F$$ with domain $$R$$ by
$$F(x,y) = \begin{cases} {f(x,y)} & {{if}(x,y){is}{in}D} \\ 0 & {{if}(x,y){is}{in}R{but}{not}{in}D} \end{cases}$$

image.alt: Details A closed loop enclosing a shaded region is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The loop resembles a rectangle with rounded sides and corners with its left side slightly larger than its right, and slightly sloping upward to the right. The top and bottom sides are slightly concave down. The region within the loop is shaded and labeled D.

Details A rectangle and an irregular shaped area are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The rectangle, labeled R, has its longer sides parallel to the x axis and is shaded. An irregular loop is drawn within the rectangle, the area within the loop is shaded in a different color and labeled D. The loop resembles a rectangle with rounded sides and corners with its left side slightly larger than its right, and slightly sloping upward to the right. The top and bottom sides are slightly concave down. The region within the loop is shaded and labeled D.

section.paragraph: If $$F$$ is integrable over $$R$$ , then we define the double integral of $$f$$ over $$D$$ by

Definition 2 makes sense because $$R$$ is a rectangle and so $$\iint_{R}{F\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ has been previously defined in Section 15.1. The procedure that we have used is reasonable because the values of $$F\left( {x,y} \right)$$ are $$0$$ when $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lies outside $$D$$ and so they contribute nothing to the integral. This means that it doesn’t matter what rectangle $$R$$ we use as long as it contains $$D$$ .

In the case where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , we can still interpret $$\iint_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ as the volume of the solid that lies above $$D$$ and under the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ (the graph of $$f$$ ). You can see that this is reasonable by comparing the graphs of $$f$$ and $$F$$ in Figures 3 and 4 and remembering that $$\iint_{R}{F\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ is the volume under the graph of $$F$$ .

section.paragraph: Figure 4 also shows that $$F$$ is likely to have discontinuities at the boundary points of $$D$$ . Nonetheless, if $$f$$ is continuous on $$D$$ and the boundary curve of $$D$$ is “well behaved”(in a sense outside the scope of this book), then it can be shown that $$\iint_{R}{F(x,y)\mathit{dA}}$$ exists and therefore $$\iint_{D}{f(x,y)\mathit{dA}}$$ exists. In particular, this is the case for the following two types of regions.
A plane region $$D$$ is said to be of type I if it lies between the graphs of two continuous functions of $$x$$ , that is,
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b,g_{1}(x) \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}(x) \right\}$$
where $$g_{1}$$ and $$g_{2}$$ are continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Some examples of type I regions are shown in Figure 5.

image.alt: Details The figure has three parts, in all three parts, two curves, labeled y = g_1(x) and y = g_2(x), a shaded region labeled D, and two vertical dashed line segments are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. There are two tick marks on the x axis: a and b, with a to the left of b. In the first part, g_1(x) begins directly above x = a, goes down to the right, concave up, reaches a low point, and then goes up the right, and ends directly over. The curve g_2(x), begins above g_1(x), directly over a, goes up to the right, concave down, reaches a high point, goes down to the right, initially concave down and then concave up, reaches a low point, goes up to the right, concave up, and ends directly over b, above the first curve. Two vertical dashed line segments rise upward from x = a and x = b, cross the starting and ending points of the first curve and reach the starting and ending points of the second curve, respectively. The region bound by the two curves and the two line segments is shaded and labeled D. In the second part, g_1 and g_2 are the bottom and top halves of a parabola opening rightward. The parabola has its vertex in the first quadrant, directly above a and its arms extend rightward until they are directly over b. The vertical dashed line segments from a and b rise until the vertex and the top arm, respectively. The region bound by the two curves and the two line segments is shaded and labeled D. In the third part, g_1 is a concave up arc between a and b. The curve g_2 begins from the same point g_1 does, slopes linearly upward to the right, reaches a peak and slopes linearly downward to the right to meet the endpoint of g_1. The region bound by the two curves is shaded and labeled D.

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: For a type I region, the functions $$g_{1}$$ and $$g_{2}$$ must be continuous but they do not need to be defined by a single formula. For instance, in the third region of Figure 5, $$g_{2}$$ is a continuous piecewise defined function.

section.paragraph: In order to evaluate $$\iint_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ when $$D$$ is a region of type I, we choose a rectangle $$R = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ that contains $$D$$ , as in Figure 6, and we let $$F$$ be the function given by Equation 1; that is, $$F$$ agrees with $$f$$ on $$D$$ and $$F$$ is $$0$$ outside $$D$$ . Then, by Fubini’s Theorem,
$${\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} =}}{\iint\limits_{R}{F\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} =}}{\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{F{\left( {x,y} \right)}dydx}}}$$
Observe that $$F\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ if $$y < g_{1}(x)$$ or $$y > g_{2}(x)$$ because $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ then lies outside $$D$$ . Therefore
because $$F{({x,y})} = f{({x,y})}$$ when $$g_{1}{(x)} \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}{(x)}$$ . Thus we have the following formula that enables us to evaluate the double integral as an iterated integral.
If $$f$$ is continuous on a type I region $$D$$ described by
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b,g_{1}(x) \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}(x) \right\}$$

section.paragraph: The integral on the right side of (3) is an iterated integral that is similar to the ones we considered in Section 15.1, except that in the inner integral we regard $$x$$ as being constant not only in $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ but also in the limits of integration, $$g_{1}(x)$$ and $$g_{2}(x)$$ .
We also consider plane regions of type II, which can be expressed as
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| c \leqslant y \leqslant d,h_{1}(y) \leqslant x \leqslant h_{2} \right.\left. (y) \right\}$$
where $$h_{1}$$ and $$h_{2}$$ are continuous. Three such regions are illustrated in Figure 7.

section.paragraph: Using the same methods that were used in establishing (3), we can show that the following result holds.
If $$f$$ is continuous on a type II region $$D$$ described by
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| c \leqslant y \leqslant d,h_{1}(y) \leqslant x \leqslant h_{2} \right.\left. (y) \right\}$$
then
$${\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} =}}{\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{h_{1}(y)}^{h_{2}(y)}{f{({x,y})}dxdy}}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the region bounded by the parabolas $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ .

Solution The parabolas intersect when $$2x^{2} = 1 + x^{2}$$ , that is, $$x^{2} = 1$$ , so $$x = \pm 1$$ . We note that the region $$D$$ , sketched in Figure 8, is a type I region but not a type II region and we can write
$$D = \left\{ (x,y) \middle| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,2x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 1 + x^{2} \right\}$$
Since the lower boundary is $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and the upper boundary is $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ , Equation 3 gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{2x^{2}}^{1 + x^{2}}{(x + 2y)dydx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2x^{2}}^{y = 1 + x^{2}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\lbrack x(1 + x^{2}) + {(1 + x^{2})}^{2} - x(2x^{2}) - {(2x^{2})}^{2}\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{( - 3x^{4} - x^{3} + 2x^{2} + x + 1)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = \left. - 3\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{4}}{4} + 2\frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right\rbrack_{- 1}^{1} = \frac{32}{15}} \end{array}$$

The first parabola is labeled y = 2 x^2, opens upward with its vertex at the origin. Its left and right arms pass through the points labeled (negative 1, 2) and (1, 2), respectively. The second parabola is labeled y = 1 + x^2, opens upward with its vertex on the positive y axis. This parabola is wider than the first and crosses the first parabola at the points (negative 1, 2) and (1, 2). The region between the two parabolas is shaded and labeled D. note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: When we set up a double integral as in Example 1, it is essential to draw a diagram. Often it is helpful to draw a vertical arrow as in Figure 8. Then the limits of integration for the inner integral can be read from the diagram as follows: The arrow starts at the lower boundary $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ , which gives the lower limit in the integral, and the arrow ends at the upper boundary $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ , which gives the upper limit of integration. For a type II region the arrow is drawn horizontally from the left boundary to the right boundary.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and above the region $$D$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane bounded by the line $$y = 2x$$ and the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ .
Solution 1 From Figure 9 we see that $$D$$ is a type I region and
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2,x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 2x \right\}$$
Therefore the volume under $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and above $$D$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}d}}A = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{x^{2}}^{2x}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {x^{2}y + \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = x^{2}}^{y = 2x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}\left\lbrack {x^{2}(2x) + \frac{(2x)^{3}}{3} - x^{2}x^{2} - \frac{\left( x^{2} \right)^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= {\int_{0}^{2}\left( {- \frac{x^{6}}{3} - x^{4} + \frac{14x^{3}}{3}} \right)}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\left. - \frac{x^{7}}{21} - \frac{x^{5}}{5} + \frac{7x^{4}}{6} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{216}{35}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A parabola, a line, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1. The parabola is labeled y = x^2, opens upward with its vertex at the origin. Its right arm passes through the point labeled (2, 4). The line is labeled y = 2 x, enters from the bottom left, slopes upward to the right passing through the origin and crossing the parabola at (2, 4), and exits at the top right. The region between the parabola and the line is shaded and labeled D. A vertical line segment is drawn connecting the parabola and the line in the first quadrant. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: Solution 2
From Figure 10 we see that $$D$$ can also be written as a type II region:
$$D = {\{{{(x,y)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 4,\frac{1}{2}y \leqslant x \leqslant \sqrt{y}}\}}}$$
Therefore another expression for $$V$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}d}}A = {\int_{0}^{4}{{\int_{\frac{1}{2}y}^{\sqrt{y}}{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dxdy}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + y^{2}x} \right\rbrack_{x = \frac{1}{2}y}^{x = \sqrt{y}}dy = {\int_{0}^{4}\left( {\frac{y^{3 \slash 2}}{3} + y^{5 \slash 2} - \frac{y^{3}}{24} - \frac{y^{3}}{2}} \right)}dy}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \left. \frac{2}{15}y^{5 \slash 2} + \frac{2}{7}y^{7 \slash 2} - \frac{13}{96}y^{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{216}{35}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A parabola, a line, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1. The parabola is labeled x = sqrt(y), opens upward with its vertex at the origin. Its right arm passes through the point labeled (2, 4). The line is labeled x = 1/2 y, enters from the bottom left, slopes upward to the right passing through the origin and crossing the parabola at (2, 4), and exits at the top right. The region between the parabola and the line is shaded and labeled D. A horizontal line segment is drawn connecting the parabola and the line in the first quadrant. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points rightward.

section.paragraph: Figure 11 shows the solid whose volume is calculated in Example 2. It lies above the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, below the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ , and between the plane $$y = 2x$$ and the parabolic cylinder $$y = x^{2}$$ .

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The parabolic cylinder, labeled z = x^2 + y^2, resembles a paraboloid shell opening upward, with its vertex at the origin, with the positive z axis as its axis. example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint\limits_{D}{xy\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the region bounded by the line $$y = x - 1$$ and the parabola $$y^{2} = 2x + 6$$ .

Solution The region $$D$$ is shown in Figure 12. Again $$D$$ is both type I and type II, but the description of $$D$$ as a type I region is more complicated because the lower boundary consists of two parts. Therefore we prefer to express $$D$$ as a type II region:
$$D = {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)| - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 4,\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3 \leqslant x \leqslant y + 1}\}}$$

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. In the first part, a parabola, a line, a shaded region, and two line segments with an arrowhead on each are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The parabola opens rightward with its vertex at (negative 3, 0) and its lower arm crosses the negative y axis just below the tick mark negative 2.The portion of the parabola above the x axis is labeled y = sqrt(2 x + 6), and passes through the point labeled (5, 4). The portion of the parabola below the x axis is labeled y = negative sqrt(2 x + 6), and passes through the point labeled (negative 1, negative 2). The line is labeled y = x minus 1, enters from the bottom, slopes upward to the right passing the points (negative 1, negative 2) and (5, 4), and exits at the top right. The region between the parabola and the line is shaded and labeled D. A vertical line segment is drawn connecting the parabola and the line in the first quadrant. An arrowhead placed on the line segment upward. Another vertical line segment is drawn connecting the two arms of the parabola, near its vertex. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points upward. In the second part, the same parabola, line, and shaded region are displayed. The parabola is labeled x = 1/2 y^2 minus 3 and the line is labeled x = y + 1. Instead of the two vertical line segments, a horizontal line segment with an arrowhead is drawn in D. The horizontal line segment begins from the parabola in the second quadrant and meets the line in the first quadrant. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points rightward.

example.paragraph: Then (4) gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\int_{\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3}^{y + 1}{\mathit{xy}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2}y} \right\rbrack_{x = \frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3}^{x = y + 1}dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- 2}^{4}{y\left\lbrack {\left( {y + 1} \right)^{2} - \left( {\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {- \frac{y^{5}}{4} + 4y^{3} + 2y^{2} - 8y} \right)}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}\mathit{xy}\mathit{dA}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {- \frac{y^{6}}{24} + y^{4} + 2\frac{y^{3}}{3} - 4y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{- 2}^{4} = 36} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: In Example 3, if we had expressed $$D$$ as a type I region using Figure 12(a), then the lower boundary curve would be
$$g_{1}(x) = \begin{cases} {- \sqrt{2x + 6}} & { \text{if} - 3 \leqslant x \leqslant - 1} \\ {x - 1} & { \text{if} - 1 < x \leqslant 5} \end{cases}$$
and we would have obtained
$$\iint\limits_{D}{xy\mathit{dA} = \int_{- 3}^{- 1}\int_{- \sqrt{2x + 6}}^{\sqrt{2x + 6}}xydydx + \int_{- 1}^{5}\int_{x - 1}^{\sqrt{2x + 6}}xydydx}$$
which would have involved more work than the other method.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the planes $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , $$x = 2y$$ , $$x = 0$$ , and $$z = 0$$ .

Solution In a question such as this, it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one of the three-dimensional solid and another of the plane region $$D$$ over which it lies. Figure 13 shows the tetrahedron $$T$$ bounded by the coordinate planes $$x = 0$$ , $$z = 0$$ , the vertical plane $$x = 2y$$ , and the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ . Since the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ intersects the $$xy$$ -plane (whose equation is $$z = 0$$ ) in the line $$x + 2y = 2$$ , we see that $$T$$ lies above the triangular region $$D$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane bounded by the lines $$x = 2y$$ , $$x + 2y = 2$$ , and $$x = 0$$ . (See Figure 14.)

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The tetrahedron is labeled T and its base lies on the first quadrant of the x y plane with its vertices at the origin and the points labeled (0, 1, 0) and (1, 1/2, 0). The top vertex of the tetrahedron is at the point labeled (0, 0, 2). The left face of the tetrahedron is labeled x = 2 y and the right face is labeled x + 2 y + z = 2. The back face is on the y z plane.

Details A triangular region and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes have a single tick mark labeled 1. The triangular region has its vertices at (0, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1/2) and is labeled D. The left side of the region is along the positive y axis. The top side, which slopes downward to the right from (0. 1) to (1, 1/2) is labeled x + 2 y = 2 or y = 1 minus x/2. The bottom side, which slopes upward to the right from the origin to (1, 1/2) is labeled y = x/2. A vertical line segment is drawn from the bottom side to the top side. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: The plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ can be written as $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ , so the required volume lies under the graph of the function $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ and above
$$D = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,x \slash 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 1 - x \slash 2} \right.}\}}}$$
Therefore

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)\mathit{dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x \slash 2}^{1 - x \slash 2}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {2y - xy - y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = x \slash 2}^{y = 1 - x \slash 2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {2 - x - x\left( {1 - \frac{x}{2}} \right) - \left( {1 - \frac{x}{2}} \right)^{2} - x + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x^{2}}{4}} \right\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\int_{0}^{1}{{({x^{2} - 2x + 1})}dx = \left. \frac{x^{3}}{3} - x^{2} + x \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Changing the Order of Integration
section.paragraph: Fubini’s Theorem tells us that we can express a double integral as an iterated integral in two different orders. Sometimes one order is much more difficult to evaluate than the other—or even impossible. The next example shows how we can change the order of integration when presented with an iterated integral that is difficult to evaluate.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Evaluate the iterated integral $$\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}dydx}}$$ .

Solution If we try to evaluate the integral as it stands, we are faced with the task of first evaluating $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ . But it’s impossible to do so in finite terms since $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ is not an elementary function. (See the end of Section 7.5.) So we must change the order of integration. This is accomplished by first expressing the given iterated integral as a double integral. Using (3) backward, we have
$$\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dA}}}}}$$
where
$$D = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,x \leqslant y \leqslant 1} \right.}\}}}$$
We sketch this region $$D$$ in Figure 15. Then from Figure 16 we see that an alternative description of $$D$$ is
$$D = \left\{ \left. {\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant x \leqslant y} \right.} \right\} \right.$$
This enables us to use (4) to express the double integral as an iterated integral in the reverse order:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dA}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{y}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {x\sin{(y^{2})}} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = y}dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{y\sin{(y^{2})}dy = \left. {- \frac{1}{2}\cos{(y^{2})}} \right\rbrack}}_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 1} \right)} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Properties of Double Integrals
section.paragraph: We assume that all of the following integrals exist. For rectangular regions $$D$$ the first three properties can be proved in the same manner as in Section 5.2. And then for general regions the properties follow from Definition 2.

$${\iint\limits_{D}{\left\lbrack {f\left( {x,y} \right) + g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rbrack\mathit{dA}}} = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} +}}{\iint\limits_{D}{g\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}}$$
$${{\iint\limits_{D}{cf\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} = c}}{\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}}} {where}c{is a constant}$$
If $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ , then
$${\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} \geqslant}}{\iint\limits_{D}{g\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}}$$

The next property of double integrals is similar to the property of single integrals given by the equation $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx = {\int_{a}^{c}{f(x)dx + {\int_{c}^{b}{f(x)dx}}}}}$$ . (Property 5 in Section 5.2).
If $$D = D_{1} \cup D_{2}$$ , where $$D_{1}$$ and $$D_{2}$$ don’t overlap except perhaps on their boundaries (see Figure 17), then
$$\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)\mathit{dA} = {\iint\limits_{D_{1}}{f(x,y)\mathit{dA} + {\iint\limits_{D_{2}}{f(x,y)\mathit{dA}}}}}}$$

image.alt: Details A region bound by a closed curve and partitioned into two is graphed in the first quadrant x y coordinate plane. The region resembles a rectangle with rounded sides and bent concave up. The region is labeled D. A curve like partition is drawn at approximately the middle of the region dividing it into two parts. The left part is labeled D_1 and the right part is labeled D_2.

section.paragraph: Property 8 can be used to evaluate double integrals over regions $$D$$ that are neither type I nor type II but can be expressed as a union of regions of type I or type II. Figure 18 illustrates this procedure. (See Exercises 67 and 68.)

image.alt: Details An irregularly shaped region within a closed curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The left side of the region is vertical. From the bottom end of the vertical side, a curve gradually goes up to the right, concave up, turns, bulges leftward and then rightward, then goes up to the left, concave down, goes down to the left, initially concave down and then concave up, reaches a low point, and then goes up to the left, initially concave up and then concave down and then meets the top end of the vertical side. The region within this closed curve is shaded and labeled D. An irregularly shaped region within a closed curve and a line segment is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The left side of the region is vertical. From the bottom end of the vertical side, a curve gradually goes up to the right, concave up, turns, bulges leftward and then rightward, then goes up to the left, concave down, goes down to the left, initially concave down and then concave up, reaches a low point, and then goes up to the left, initially concave up and then concave down and then meets the top end of the vertical side. The region within this closed curve is shaded. A vertical line segment is drawn connecting the top and bottom parts of the curve, near its bulging portions. The part of the shaded region to the left of the line segment is labeled D_1 and the part on the right is labeled D_2.

section.paragraph: The next property of integrals says that if we integrate the constant function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 1$$ over a region $$D$$ , we get the area of $$D$$ :
$$\iint\limits_{D}{1\mathit{dA} = A(D)}$$

Figure 19 illustrates why Equation 9 is true: A solid cylinder whose base is $$D$$ and whose height is $$1$$ has volume $$A(D) \cdot 1 = A(D)$$ , but we know that we can also write its volume as $$\iint_{D}{1\mathit{dA}}$$ .

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of an irregular cylinder is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The base and the top side of the cylinder resemble the shape of a kidney. The cylinder has a height of 1 unit and its top side is labeled z = 1.

section.paragraph: Finally, we can combine Properties 6, 7, and 9 to prove the following property. (See Exercise 73.)
If $$m \leqslant f\left( {x,y} \right) \leqslant M$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ , then
$$m \cdot A(D) \leqslant {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} \leqslant M \cdot A(D)}}$$

Figure 20 illustrates Property 10 for the case $$m > 0$$ . The volume of the solid below the graph of $$z = f(x,y)$$ and above $$D$$ is between the volumes of the cylinders with base $$D$$ and heights $$m$$ and $$M$$ . (Compare to Figure 5.2.17, which illustrates the analogous property for single integrals.)

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of an irregular cylinder, two points, and four surfaces are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The base and the top side of the cylinder resemble the shape of a kidney. The bottom surface is labeled D. The top surface is labeled z = M. A point is marked on the left side of this surface. Another horizontal surface parallel and of the same size of the top surface is shaded below the top surface and labeled z = m. A point is marked on the right side of this surface. The fourth surface begins from the top left edge of the cylinder, includes the point on z = M, goes down to the right, reaches a minimum at the point on z = m and then briefly rises up once again.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Use Property 10 to estimate the integral $$\iint_{D}{e^{\sin x\cos y}\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the disk with center the origin and radius $$2$$ .

Solution Since $$- 1 \leqslant \sin x \leqslant 1$$ and $$- 1 \leqslant \cos y \leqslant 1$$ , we have $$- 1 \leqslant \sin x\cos y \leqslant 1$$ and, because the natural exponential function is increasing, we have
$$e^{- 1} \leqslant e^{\sin x\cos y} \leqslant e^{1} = e$$
Thus, using $$m = e^{- 1} = 1 \slash e$$ , $$M = e$$ , and $$A(D) = \pi(2)^{2}$$ in Property 10, we obtain
$$\frac{4\pi}{e} \leqslant {\iint\limits_{D}{e^{\sin x\cos y}\mathit{dA} \leqslant 4\pi e}}$$

exercises.instruction: 11, 12, 13, and 14 Evaluate the double integral.

section.heading: 15.3. Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: Suppose that we want to evaluate a double integral $$\iint_{R}{f(x,y)dA}$$ , where the region $$R$$ is a circular disk centered at the origin. In this case the description of $$R$$ in terms of rectangular coordinates is rather complicated, but $$R$$ is readily described using polar coordinates. In general, if $$R$$ is a region that is more easily described using polar coordinates, it is often advantageous to evaluate the double integral by first converting it to polar coordinates.
section.heading: Review of Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: Polar coordinates were introduced in Section 10.3. Recall from Figure 1 that the polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ of a point are related to the rectangular coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ of that point by the equations
$${r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}} {x = r\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta}$$

Equations of circles centered at the origin are particularly simple in polar coordinates. The unit circle has equation $$r - 1$$ ; the region enclosed by this circle is shown in Figure 2(a). Figure 2(b) illustrates another region that is conveniently described in polar coordinates.

image.alt: Details Three line segments forming a right triangle are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The first line segment, labeled r, slopes upward to the right from the origin at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from the x axis until a point labeled P(r, theta) = P(x, y). From this point, labeled y, a vertical line segment descends downward to meet the x axis. The third line segment, labeled x, runs along the x axis from the origin to the point where the vertical line segment y meets the x axis. The three line segments form a right triangle with a horizontal base x, vertical side on the right y, and the hypotenuse r sloping downward to the left. The angle between x and y is a right angle.

Details A circle is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The circle is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 1 and has its center at the origin. The region within the circle is shaded and labeled R. A semicircular ring is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The ring rests on the x axis and has its center at origin. The outer boundary of the ring is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 4 and the inner boundary is labeled x62 + y^2 = 1. The region between the outer and inner boundary of the ring is shaded and labeled R.

section.paragraph: You may wish to review Table 10.3.1 for other common curves suitably described in polar coordinates.
section.heading: Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: The regions in Figure 2 are special cases of a polar rectangle
$$R = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| a \leqslant r \leqslant b,\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta \right\}$$

which is shown in Figure 3. In order to compute the double integral $$\iint_{R}{f(x,y)dA}$$ , where $$R$$ is a polar rectangle, we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$m$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {r_{i - 1},r_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta r = \left( {b - a} \right) \slash m$$ and we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {\alpha,\beta} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {\theta_{j - 1},\theta_{j}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta\theta = \left( {\beta - \alpha} \right) \slash n$$ . Then the circles $$r = r_{i}$$ and the rays $$\theta = \theta_{j}$$ divide the polar rectangle $$R$$ into the small polar rectangles $$R_{ij}$$ shown in Figure 4.

image.alt: Details A polar rectangle is graphed in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. It resembles a sector cut from two concentric circles or a trapezium bulging outward from the origin. The trapezium has a short bottom side and a longer top side and is at a distance away from the origin as if they are a portion of two concentric circles. The bottom side is labeled r = a and the top side is labeled r = b. A dashed line segment begins from the origin at an angle alpha from the positive horizontal axis, slopes upward to the right, and meets the bottom right corner of the trapezium. The right side of the trapezium is labeled theta = alpha. Another dashed line segment begins from the origin at an angle beta from the positive horizontal axis, slopes steeply upward to the right, and meets the bottom left corner of the trapezium. The left side of the trapezium is labeled theta = beta. The curved trapezium is shaded and labeled R.

Details A polar rectangle graphed in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane is divided into smaller rectangles. Dashed line segments begin from the origin and slope upward to the right to meet the bottom of the polar rectangle and continue as solid lines dividing the rectangle into radial strips. Consecutive line segments have increasing slope and the angle between two consecutive line segments is Delta theta. Arcs parallel to the top and bottom sides of the polar rectangle, evenly spaced, begin from the left edge and end at the right edge, dividing the rectangle into curved strips of equal width. Thus, the polar rectangle is divided into smaller polar rectangles. One of the rectangles is shaded and labeled R_(i j). It lies between the lower arc labeled r = r_(i minus 1) and the upper arc labeled r = r_i and between the left line segment labeled theta = theta _j and the right line segment theta = theta_(j minus 1). A dot is placed at the center of the shaded rectangle and labeled (r^*_i, theta^*_j).

section.paragraph: Compare Figure 4 with Figure 15.1.3.
The “center” of the polar subrectangle
$$R_{ij} = \left\{ (r,\theta) \middle| r_{i - 1} \leqslant r \leqslant r_{i},\theta_{j - 1} \leqslant \theta \leqslant \theta_{j} \right\}$$
has polar coordinates

We compute the area of $$R_{ij}$$ using the fact that the area of a sector of a circle with radius $$r$$ and central angle $$\theta$$ is $$\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta$$ . Subtracting the areas of two such sectors, each of which has central angle $$\Delta\theta = \theta_{j} - \theta_{j - 1}$$ , we find that the area of $$R_{ij}$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta A_{i} = \frac{1}{2}r_{i}^{2}\Delta\theta - \frac{1}{2}r_{i - 1}^{2}\Delta\theta = \frac{1}{2}(r_{i}^{2} - r_{i - 1}^{2})\Delta\theta} \\ {\phantom{\Delta A_{i}} = \frac{1}{2}(r_{i} + r_{i - 1})(r_{i} - r_{i - 1})\Delta\theta = r_{i}^{*}\Delta r\Delta\theta} \end{array}$$

Although we have defined the double integral $$\iint_{R}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ in terms of ordinary rectangles, it can be shown that, for continuous functions $$f$$ , we always obtain the same answer using polar rectangles. The rectangular coordinates of the center of $$R_{ij}$$ are $$({r_{i}^{*}\cos\theta_{j}^{*},r_{i}^{*}\sin\theta_{j}^{*}})$$ , so a typical Riemann sum is

$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f{({r_{i}^{*}\cos\theta_{j}^{*},r_{i}^{*}\sin\theta_{j}^{*}})}\Delta A_{i}}} = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f{({r_{i}^{*}\cos\theta_{j}^{*},r_{i}^{*}\sin\theta_{j}^{*}})}r_{i}^{*}\Delta r\Delta\theta}}$$
If we write $$g\left( {r,\theta} \right) = rf\left( {r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta} \right)$$ , then the Riemann sum in Equation 1 can be written as
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{g{({r_{i}^{*},\theta_{j}^{*}})}\Delta r\Delta\theta}}$$
which is a Riemann sum for the double integral
$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\int_{a}^{b}{g\left( {r,\theta} \right)drd\theta}}$$
Therefore we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}f(r_{i}^{*}\cos\theta_{j}^{*},r_{i}^{*}\sin\theta_{j}^{*}){\Delta A_{i}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}g(r_{i}^{*},\theta_{j}^{*}){\Delta r}{\Delta\theta} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b}g(r,\theta)drd\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}f(x,y)dA} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b}f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)rdrd\theta} \end{array}$$

note.source_type: Change to Polar Coodinates in a Double Integral
note.title: Change to Polar Coodinates in a Double Integral
note.heading: Change to Polar Coodinates in a Double Integral
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on a polar rectangle $$R$$ given by $$0 \leqslant a \leqslant r \leqslant b$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$0 \leqslant \beta - a \leqslant 2\pi$$ , then
$${\iint\limits_{R}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} =}}{\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta} \right)rdrd\theta}}}$$

section.paragraph: The formula in (2) says that we convert from rectangular to polar coordinates in a double integral by writing $$x = r\cos\theta$$ and $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , using the appropriate limits of integration for $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ , and replacing $$\mathit{dA}$$ by $$rdrd\theta$$ . Be careful not to forget the additional factor $$r$$ on the right side of Formula 2. A classical method for remembering this is shown in Figure 5, where the “infinitesimal” polar rectangle can be thought of as an ordinary rectangle with dimensions $$rd\theta$$ and $$dr$$ and therefore has “area” $$\mathit{dA} = rdrd\theta$$ .

image.alt: Details A polar rectangle and two line segments are graphed in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. A very small polar rectangle is drawn in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. A dashed line segment, labeled r, begins at the origin, slopes upward to the right and meets the bottom right corner of the polar rectangle. Another line segment, at an angle d theta to the first, slopes upward to the right, more steeply than the first, and meets the bottom left corner of the polar rectangle. The bottom side of the rectangle is labeled r d theta. The right side of the rectangle is labeled d r. The area within the rectangle is shaded and labeled d A.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{R}{({3x + 4y^{2}})}\mathit{dA}$$ , where $$R$$ is the region in the upper half-plane bounded by the circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ .
Solution The region $$R$$ can be described as
$$R = {\{{{\left( {x,y} \right){|{y \geqslant 0,1 \leqslant x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 4}}}\}}}$$
It is the half-ring shown in Figure 2(b), and in polar coordinates it is given by $$1 \leqslant r \leqslant 2$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . Therefore, by Formula 2,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}\lbrack 3(r\cos\theta) + 4{(r\sin\theta)}^{2}\rbrack rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}(3r^{2}\cos\theta + 4r^{3}\sin^{2}\theta)drd\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack r^{3}\cos\theta + r^{4}\sin^{2}\theta \right\rbrack_{r = 1}^{r = 2}d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi}(7\cos\theta + 15\sin^{2}\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\lbrack 7\cos\theta + \frac{15}{2}(1 - \cos 2\theta)\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{R}(3x + 4y^{2})dA} = \left. {7\sin\theta + \frac{15\theta}{2} - \frac{15}{4}\sin 2\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = \frac{15\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$
Here we use the trigonometric identity
$$\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {1 - \cos 2\theta} \right)}$$
See Section 7.2 for advice on integrating trigonometric functions.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate the double integral
Solution This iterated integral is a double integral over the region $$R$$ shown in Figure 6 and described by
$$R = \{(x,y)| - 1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\}$$
The region is a half-disk, so it is more simply described in polar coordinates:
$$R = \{(r,\theta)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1\}$$
Therefore we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}(x^{2} + y^{2})\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(r^{2})r\mathit{dr}\mathit{d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right)\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} = \int_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{r = 0}^{r = 1}\mathit{d\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\pi}\mathit{d\theta} = \frac{\pi}{4}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A semicircular region is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The region is bound by a semicircle and the x axis. The semicircle is labeled y = sqrt(1 minus x^2, has its center at the origin, meets the x axis at (1, 0), and crosses the y axis at (0, 1). The region between the semicircle and the x axis is shaded and labeled R.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid bounded by the plane $$z = 0$$ and the paraboloid $$z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ .

Solution If we put $$z = 0$$ in the equation of the paraboloid, we get $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . This means that the plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , so the solid lies under the paraboloid and above the circular disk $$D$$ given by $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1$$ [see Figures 7 and 2(a)]. In polar coordinates $$D$$ is given by $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Since $$1 - x^{2} - y^{2} = 1 - r^{2}$$ , the volume is

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{D}(1 - x^{2} - y^{2})dA = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(1 - r^{2})rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{1}(r - r^{3})dr = 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{r^{2}}{2} - \frac{r^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a paraboloid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The paraboloid has its vertex at (0, 0, 1) and opens downward until the x y plane. The circular base of the paraboloid on the x y plane is shaded and labeled D. The vertical traces on the surface of the paraboloid on the x z plane and y z plane are parabolas opening downward sharing their vertices with the paraboloid.

section.paragraph: In Example 3, if we had used rectangular coordinates instead of polar coordinates, we would have obtained
$$V = \iint\limits_{D}(1 - x^{2} - y^{2})\mathit{dA} = \int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{- \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}(1 - x^{2} - y^{2})\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$
which is not easy to evaluate because it involves finding $$\int{({1 - x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}dx$$ .

What we have done so far can be extended to the more complicated type of region shown in Figure 8. It’s similar to the type II rectangular regions we considered in Section 15.2. In fact, by combining Formula 2 in this section with Formula 15.2.4, we obtain the following formula.

image.alt: Details A polar rectangle is graphed in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The top and bottom sides are not smooth and resemble wavy irregular curves. The bottom side is labeled r = h_1(theta) and the top side is labeled r = h_2(theta). A dashed line segment begins from the origin at an angle alpha from the positive horizontal axis, slopes upward to the right, and meets the bottom right corner of the trapezium. The right side of the trapezium is labeled theta = alpha. Another dashed line segment begins from the origin at an angle beta from the positive horizontal axis, slopes steeply upward to the right, and meets the bottom left corner of the trapezium. The left side of the trapezium is labeled theta = beta. The curved trapezium is shaded and labeled D. A line segment with an arrowhead is drawn from the bottom side to the top side and is oriented radially outward from the origin. The arrowhead points toward the top side.

section.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on a polar region of the form
$$D = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| \alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta,h_{1}(\theta) \leqslant r \leqslant h_{2}(\theta) \right\}$$
then
$$\iint\limits_{D}f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{h_{1}{(\theta)}}^{h_{2}{(\theta)}}f\left( {r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta} \right)rdrd\theta$$

In particular, taking $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 1$$ , $$h_{1}(\theta) = 0$$ , and $$h_{2}(\theta) = h(\theta)$$ in this formula, we see that the area of the region $$D$$ bounded by $$\theta = \alpha$$ , $$\theta = \beta$$ , and $$r = h(\theta)$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A(D) = \iint\limits_{D}1\mathit{dA} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{h{(\theta)}}rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{A(D)} = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{h(\theta)}d\theta = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {h(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta} \end{array}$$
and this agrees with Formula 10.4.3.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use a double integral to find the area enclosed by one loop of the four-leaved rose $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ .
Solution From the sketch of the curve in Figure 9, we see that a loop is given by the region
$$D = \left\{ \left. {\left( {r,\theta} \right)\left. \middle| {- \pi \slash 4 \leqslant \theta \leqslant} \right.\pi \slash 4,0 \leqslant r \leqslant \cos 2\theta} \right\} \right.$$
So the area is

$$\begin{array}{l} {{A(D)} = \iint\limits_{D}\mathit{dA} = \int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\int_{0}^{\cos 2\theta}rdrd\theta} \\ {\phantom{A(D)} = \int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}r^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\cos 2\theta}d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}\cos^{2}2\theta d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A(D)} = \frac{1}{4}\int_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4}(1 + \cos 4\theta)d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {\theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 4\theta} \right\rbrack_{- \pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 4} = \frac{\pi}{8}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A four leaved rose and two dashed lines are graphed in a coordinate plane. The four leaves are arranged one each on the positive and negative horizontal and vertical axes, symmetric about them. The first dashed line begins from the origin, slopes upward to the right and is labeled theta = pi/4. The second dashed line begins from the origin, slopes downward to the right and is labeled theta = negative pi/4.

Solution The solid lies above the disk $$D$$ whose boundary circle has equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x$$ or, after completing the square,
(See Figures 10 and 11.)

Details Three dimensional renderings of a cylinder and a paraboloid are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The paraboloid, labeled z = x^2 + y^2, opens upward and has its vertex at the origin.
