example.paragraph: In polar coordinates we have $$x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}$$ and $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , so the boundary circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 2x$$ becomes $$r^{2} = 2r\cos\theta$$ , or $$r = 2\cos\theta$$ . Thus the disk $$D$$ is given by
$$D = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| - \pi \slash 2 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \slash 2,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2\cos\theta \right\}$$
and, by Formula 3, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = \iint\limits_{D}({x^{2} + y^{2}})\mathit{dA} = \int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\int_{0}^{2\cos\theta}r^{2}rdrd\theta = \int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\cos\theta}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 4\int_{- \pi \slash 2}^{\pi \slash 2}\cos^{4}\theta d\theta = 8\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\cos^{4}\theta d\theta = 8\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left( \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2} \right)^{2}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 2\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left\lbrack {1 + 2\cos 2\theta + \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 4\theta} \right)} \right\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{V} = 2\left\lbrack {\frac{3}{2}\theta + \sin 2\theta + \frac{1}{8}\sin 4\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 2} = 2\left( \frac{3}{2} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \frac{3\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: 15.4. Applications of Double Integrals
section.paragraph: We have already seen one application of double integrals: computing volumes. Another geometric application is finding areas of surfaces and this will be done in the next section. In this section we explore physical applications such as computing mass, electric charge, center of mass, and moment of inertia. We will see that these physical ideas are also important when applied to probability density functions of two random variables.
section.heading: Density and Mass
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3 we were able to use single integrals to compute moments and the center of mass of a thin plate or lamina with constant density. But now, equipped with the double integral, we can consider a lamina with variable density. Suppose the lamina occupies a region $$D$$ of the $$xy$$ -plane and its density (in units of mass per unit area) at a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ is given by $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$\rho$$ is a continuous function on $$D$$ . This means that
$$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \lim\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta A}$$

where $$\Delta m$$ and $$\Delta A$$ are the mass and area of a small rectangle that contains $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and the limit is taken as the dimensions of the rectangle approach 0. (See Figure 1.)

image.alt: Details A rectangular grid, a closed curve, a shaded region, a square, and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. An irregular closed curve is drawn in the first quadrant within a rectangular grid such that its extreme points touch the sides of the grid. The region within the curve is shaded. One of the cells of the grid within the curve is shaded with a different color. An enlarged view of the cell shows a square with a point within. The square is labeled r_(i j) and the point is labeled (x^*_(i j), y^*_(i j)).

section.paragraph: To find the total mass $$m$$ of the lamina we divide a rectangle $$R$$ containing $$D$$ into subrectangles $$R_{ij}$$ of the same size (as in Figure 2) and consider $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to be $$0$$ outside $$D$$ . If we choose a point $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in $$R_{\mathit{ij}}$$ , then the mass of the part of the lamina that occupies $$R_{ij}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A$$ , where $$\Delta A$$ is the area of $$R_{ij}$$ . If we add all such masses, we get an approximation to the total mass:
$$m \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{k}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}{\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A}}$$

figure.caption: The mass of each subrectangle $$R_{\mathit{ij}}$$ is approximated by $$\rho(x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*})\Delta A$$ .

section.paragraph: If we now increase the number of subrectangles, we obtain the total mass $$m$$ of the lamina as the limiting value of the approximations:
$$m = \lim\limits_{k,l\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{k}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}{\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A =}}{\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

Physicists also consider other types of density that can be treated in the same manner. For example, if an electric charge is distributed over a region $$D$$ and the charge density (in units of charge per unit area) is given by $$\sigma\left( {x,y} \right)$$ at a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ , then the total electric charge $$Q$$ is given by
$$Q = {\iint\limits_{D}\sigma}\left( {x,y} \right)dA$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Charge is distributed over the triangular region $$D$$ in Figure 3 so that the charge density at $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$\sigma\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ , measured in coulombs per square meter $$(C \slash m^{2})$$ . Find the total charge.

image.alt: Details A triangle, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The triangle is a right triangle with its vertices at (1, 1), (1,0), and (0, 1). The top side of the triangle is labeled y = 1 and the bottom side which slopes downward to the right from (0, 1) to (1, 0) is labeled y = 1 minus x. The region within the triangle is shaded and labeled D. A vertical line segment is drawn from the bottom side to the top side and an arrow head placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: Solution From Equation 2 and Figure 3 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {Q = {\iint\limits_{D}\sigma}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{1 - x}^{1}{xy}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 1 - x}^{y = 1}dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x}{2}{\lbrack{1^{2} - \left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}}\rbrack}}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({2x^{2} - x^{3}})dx}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{2x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{5}{24}}} \end{array}$$
Thus the total charge is $$\frac{5}{24}C$$ .

section.heading: Moments and Centers of Mass
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3 we found the center of mass of a lamina with constant density; here we consider a lamina with variable density. Suppose the lamina occupies a region $$D$$ and has density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . Recall from Chapter 8 that we defined the moment of a particle about an axis as the product of its mass and its directed distance from the axis. We divide $$D$$ into small rectangles as in Figure 2. Then the mass of $$R_{ij}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A$$ , so we can approximate the moment of $$R_{ij}$$ with respect to the $$x$$ -axis by
$${\lbrack{\rho{({x_{ij,}^{\ast}y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}\rbrack}y_{ij}^{\ast}$$
If we now add these quantities and take the limit as the number of subrectangles becomes large, we obtain the moment of the entire lamina about the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis:

$$M_{x} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}y_{ij}^{\ast}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$
Similarly, the moment about the $$\mathbf{y}$$ -axis is

$$M_{y} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}x_{ij}^{\ast}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

As before, we define the center of mass $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ so that $$m\overline{x} = M_{y}$$ and $$m\overline{y} = M_{x}$$ . The physical significance is that the lamina behaves as if its entire mass is concentrated at its center of mass. Thus the lamina balances horizontally when supported at its center of mass (see Figure 4).

image.alt: Details A flat solid, labeled D, resembling the sole of a shoe is displayed. A thin tall cone is placed below the solid with its tip touching a point labeled (x bar, y bar) on the broader side of the solid.

section.paragraph: The coordinates $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ of the center of mass of a lamina occupying the region $$D$$ and having density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ are
$${\overline{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA} {\overline{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA}$$
where the mass $$m$$ is given by
$$m = {\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the mass and center of mass of a triangular lamina with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ if the density function is $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + 3x + y$$ .
Solution The triangle is shown in Figure 5. (Note that the equation of the upper boundary is $$y = 2 - 2x$$ .) The mass of the lamina is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}\left( {1 + 3x + y} \right)}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {y + 3xy + \frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{m} = 4{\int_{0}^{1}{({1 - x^{2}})}}dx = 4\left\lbrack {x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{8}{3}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A triangular region and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The region rests on the x axis with its vertices at (0, 0), (0, 2), and (1, 0). The hypotenuse is labeled y = 2 minus 2 x. The triangular region is labeled D. A point at the center of the triangle is labeled (?, 11/16).

example.paragraph: Then the formulas in (5) give

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{x} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({x + 3x^{2} + xy})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + 3x^{2}y + x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({x - x^{3}})}}dx = \frac{3}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{3}{8}} \\ {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({y + 3xy + y^{2}})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2}}{2} + 3x\frac{y^{2}}{2} + \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx = \frac{1}{4}{\int_{0}^{1}{({7 - 9x - 3x^{2} + 5x^{3}})}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {7x - 9\frac{x^{2}}{2} - x^{3} + 5\frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{11}{16}} \end{array}$$
The center of mass is at the point $$\left( {\frac{3}{8},\frac{11}{16}} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: The density at any point on a semicircular lamina is proportional to the distance from the center of the circle. Find the center of mass of the lamina.

Solution Let’s place the lamina as the upper half of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ . (See Figure 6.) Then the distance from a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to the center of the circle (the origin) is $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ . Therefore the density function is
$$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$

where $$K$$ is some constant. Both the density function and the shape of the lamina suggest that we convert to polar coordinates. Then $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = r$$ and the region $$D$$ is given by $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . Thus the mass of the lamina is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}\rho}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}}dA} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta = K{\int_{0}^{\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{a}{r^{2}dr}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = K\pi\left. \frac{r^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{K\pi a^{3}}{3}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A semicircular region is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The boundary of the region has a horizontal base along the x axis from (negative a, 0) to (a, 0) and the semicircular arch crosses the y axis at (0, a). The arch is labeled x^2 + y^2 = a. The region within the boundary is shaded and labeled D. A point marked on the y axis is labeled (0, (3 a)/(2 pi)).

example.paragraph: Both the lamina and the density function are symmetric with respect to the $$y$$ -axis, so the center of mass must lie on the $$y$$ -axis, that is, $$\overline{x} = 0$$ . The $$y$$ -coordinate is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = \frac{3}{K\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{r\sin\theta\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin\theta d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}}dr =}}\frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\left\lbrack {- \cos\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\frac{2a^{4}}{4} = \frac{3a}{2\pi}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the center of mass is located at the point $$\left( {0,3a \slash \left( {2\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

Compare the location of the center of mass in Example 3 with Example 8.3.4, where we found that the center of mass of a lamina with the same shape but uniform density is located at the point $$\left( {0,4a \slash \left( {3\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

section.heading: Moment of Inertia
section.paragraph: The moment of inertia (also called the second moment) of a particle of mass $$m$$ about an axis is defined to be $$mr^{2}$$ , where $$r$$ is the distance from the particle to the axis. We extend this concept to a lamina with density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and occupying a region $$D$$ by proceeding as we did for ordinary moments. We divide $$D$$ into small rectangles, approximate the moment of inertia of each subrectangle about the $$x$$ -axis, and take the limit of the sum as the number of subrectangles becomes large. The result is the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis:

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{x} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{{(y_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}}} \\ { = {\iint\limits_{D}{y^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} \end{array}$$
Similarly, the moment of inertia about the $$\mathbf{y}$$ -axis is

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{y} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{{(x_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast})}^{2}\rho{({x_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast},y_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}}} \\ { = {\iint\limits_{D}{x^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} \end{array}$$
We also consider the moment of inertia about the origin, also called the polar moment of inertia:

$$I_{0} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\left\lbrack {{(x_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2} + {(y_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2}} \right\rbrack\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}}$$
Note that $$I_{0} = I_{x} + I_{y}$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the moments of inertia $$I_{x}$$ , $$I_{y}$$ , and $$I_{0}$$ of a homogeneous disk $$D$$ with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \rho$$ , center the origin, and radius $$a$$ .

Solution The boundary of $$D$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ and in polar coordinates $$D$$ is described by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ . By Formula 6,

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{x} = {\iint\limits_{D}{y^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\sin\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin^{2}\theta}d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2\theta})d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \frac{\rho}{2}\left\lbrack \theta - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$
Similarly, Formula 7 gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{y} = {\iint\limits_{D}{x^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\cos\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{y}} = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)d\theta\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$
(From the symmetry of the problem, it is expected that $$I_{x} = I_{y}$$ .) We could use Formula 8 to compute $$I_{0}$$ directly, or use

section.paragraph: In Example 4 notice that the mass of the disk is
$$m = {density} \times {area} = \rho{({\pi a^{2}})}$$
so the moment of inertia of the disk about the origin (like a wheel about its axle) can be written as

Thus if we increase the mass or the radius of the disk, we thereby increase the moment of inertia. In general, the moment of inertia plays much the same role in rotational motion that mass plays in linear motion. The moment of inertia of a wheel is what makes it difficult to start or stop the rotation of the wheel, just as the mass of a car is what makes it difficult to start or stop the motion of the car.
The radius of gyration of a lamina about an axis is the number $$R$$ such that

where $$m$$ is the mass of the lamina and $$I$$ is the moment of inertia about the given axis. Equation 9 says that if the mass of the lamina were concentrated at a distance $$R$$ from the axis, then the moment of inertia of this “point mass” would be the same as the moment of inertia of the lamina.
In particular, the radius of gyration $$\overset{=}{y}$$ with respect to the $$x$$ -axis and the radius of gyration $$\overset{=}{x}$$ with respect to the $$y$$ -axis are given by the equations

Thus $$({\overset{=}{x},\overset{=}{y}})$$ is the point at which the mass of the lamina can be concentrated without changing the moments of inertia with respect to the coordinate axes. (Note the analogy with the center of mass.)

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the radius of gyration about the $$x$$ -axis of the disk in Example 4.
Solution As noted, the mass of the disk is $$m = \rho\pi a^{2}$$ , so from Equations 10 we have
Therefore the radius of gyration about the $$x$$ -axis is $$\overset{=}{y} = \frac{1}{2}a$$ , which is half the radius of the disk.

section.heading: Probability
section.paragraph: In Section 8.5 we considered the probability density function $$f$$ of a continuous random variable $$X$$ . This means that $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , $$\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f{(x)}dx = 1}$$ , and the probability that $$X$$ lies between $$a$$ and $$b$$ is found by integrating $$f$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ :
$$P\left( {a \leqslant X \leqslant b} \right) = {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$

Now we consider a pair of continuous random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , such as the lifetimes of two components of a machine or the height and weight of an adult female chosen at random. The joint density function of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ is a function $$f$$ of two variables such that the probability that $$\left( {X,Y} \right)$$ lies in a region $$D$$ is
$$P\left( {\left( {X,Y} \right) \in D} \right) = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$
In particular, if the region is a rectangle, then the probability that $$X$$ lies between $$a$$ and $$b$$ and $$Y$$ lies between $$c$$ and $$d$$ is
$$P\left( {a \leqslant X \leqslant b,c \leqslant Y \leqslant d} \right) = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}}$$
(See Figure 7.)

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid has a rectangular base which lies on the x y plane. Its longer sides are parallel to the y axis. The base is shaded and labeled D. Two dashed line segments begin from x = a and x = b on the positive x axis, run parallel to the y axis, and meet the top and bottom left corners of the rectangular base. Two more dashed line segments begin from y = c and y = d on the positive y axis, run parallel to the x axis, and meet the top left and right corners of the rectangular base. The top surface of the solid is at a certain height from the base, is labeled z = f(x, y), and is a rectangle curved concave down. The remaining four sides of the solid complete the figure with three linear and a curved top side.

figure.caption: The probability that $$X$$ lies between $$a$$ and $$b$$ and $$Y$$ lies between $$c$$ and $$d$$ is the volume that lies above the rectangle $$D = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ and below the graph of the joint density function.

section.paragraph: Because probabilities aren’t negative and are measured on a scale from $$0$$ to $$1$$ , the joint density function has the following properties:
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0 {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = 1}}$$
As in Exercise 15.3.50, the double integral over $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ is an improper integral defined as the limit of double integrals over expanding circles or squares, and we can write
$${\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = 1}}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: If the joint density function for $$X$$ and $$Y$$ is given by
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \begin{cases} {C\left( {x + 2y} \right)} & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 10,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 10} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$
find the value of the constant $$C$$ . Then find $$P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right)$$ .

Solution We find the value of $$C$$ by ensuring that the double integral of $$f$$ over $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ is equal to $$1$$ . Because $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ outside the rectangle $$\left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}} = {\int_{0}^{10}{\int_{0}^{10}{C\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx = C{\int_{0}^{10}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 10}}}}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = C{\int_{0}^{10}{{\left( {10x + 100} \right)}dx = 1500C}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore $$1500C = 1$$ and so $$C = \frac{1}{1500}$$ .
Now we can compute the probability that $$X$$ is at most $$7$$ and $$Y$$ is at least $$2$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right) = {\int_{- \infty}^{7}{\int_{2}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = {\int_{0}^{7}{\int_{2}^{10}{\frac{1}{1500}\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2}^{y = 10}dx = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}{\left( {8x + 96} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{868}{1500} \approx 0.5787} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Suppose $$X$$ is a random variable with probability density function $$f_{1}(x)$$ and $$Y$$ is a random variable with density function $$f_{2}(y)$$ . Then $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are called independent random variables if their joint density function is the product of their individual density functions:
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)$$
In Section 8.5 we modeled waiting times by using exponential density functions
$$f(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}t < 0} \\ {\mu^{- 1}e^{- t \slash \mu}} & {{if}t \geqslant 0} \end{cases}$$
where $$\mu$$ is the mean waiting time. In the next example we consider a situation with two independent waiting times.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: The manager of a movie theater determines that the average time moviegoers wait in line to buy a ticket for a film is $$10$$ minutes and the average time they wait to buy popcorn is $$5$$ minutes. Assuming that the waiting times are independent, find the probability that a moviegoer waits a total of less than $$20$$ minutes before taking his or her seat.

Solution Assuming that both the waiting time $$X$$ for the ticket purchase and the waiting time $$Y$$ in the refreshment line are modeled by exponential probability density functions, we can write the individual density functions as

$$f_{1}(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & {{if}x < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{10}e^{- x \slash 10}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \end{array} f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}y < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{5}e^{- y \slash 5}} & {{if}y \geqslant 0} \end{cases} \right.$$
Since $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are independent, the joint density function is the product:
$$f(x,y) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} {\frac{1}{50}{e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0,y \geqslant 0} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$
We are asked for the probability that $$X + Y < 20$$ :
$$P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = P\left( {\left( {X,Y} \right) \in D} \right)$$
where $$D$$ is the triangular region shown in Figure 8. Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = {\int_{0}^{20}{\int_{0}^{20 - x}{\frac{1}{50}e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = \frac{1}{50}\int_{0}^{20}\left\lbrack {e^{- x \slash 10}\left( {- 5} \right)e^{- y \slash 5}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 20 - x}dx} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{e^{- x \slash 10}{({1 - e^{{({x - 20})} \slash 5}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{{({e^{- x \slash 10} - e^{- 4}e^{ x \slash 10}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = 1 + e^{- 4} - 2e^{- 2} \approx 0.7476} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A triangular region and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The region rests on the x axis with its vertices at (0, 0), (0, 20), and (20, 0). The hypotenuse is labeled x + y = 20. The triangular region is labeled D.

example.paragraph: This means that about $$75\%$$ of the moviegoers wait less than $$20$$ minutes before taking their seats.

section.heading: Expected Values
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 8.5 that if $$X$$ is a random variable with probability density function $$f$$ , then its mean is
$$\mu = {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xf(x)dx}}$$
Now if $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are random variables with joint density function $$f$$ , we define the $$\mathbf{X}$$ -mean and $$\mathbf{Y}$$ -mean, also called the expected values of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , to be
$${\mu_{1} = {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{xf\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} {\mu_{2} = {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{yf\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}$$

Notice how closely the expressions for $$\mu_{1}$$ and $$\mu_{2}$$ in (11) resemble the moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}$$ of a lamina with density function $$\rho$$ in Equations 3 and 4. In fact, we can think of probability as being like continuously distributed mass. We calculate probability the way we calculate mass—by integrating a density function. And because the total “probability mass” is $$1$$ , the expressions for $$\overline{x}$$ and $$\overline{y}$$ in (5) show that we can think of the expected values of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , $$\mu_{1}$$ and $$\mu_{2}$$ , as the coordinates of the “center of mass” of the probability distribution.
In the next example we deal with normal distributions. As in Section 8.5, a single random variable is normally distributed if its probability density function is of the form
where $$\mu$$ is the mean and $$\sigma$$ is the standard deviation.

section.heading: 15.5. Surface Area
section.paragraph: In this section we apply double integrals to the problem of computing the area of a surface. In Section 8.2 we found the area of a very special type of surface––a surface of revolution––by the methods of single-variable calculus. Here we compute the area of a surface with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , the graph of a function of two variables.
In Section 16.6 we will deal with areas of more general surfaces, called parametric surfaces, and so this section may be omitted if that later section will be covered.

Let $$S$$ be a surface with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$f$$ has continuous partial derivatives. For simplicity in deriving the surface area formula, we assume that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ and the domain $$D$$ of $$f$$ is a rectangle. We divide $$D$$ into small rectangles $$R_{ij}$$ with area $$\Delta A = \Delta x\Delta y$$ . If $$\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)$$ is the corner of $$R_{ij}$$ closest to the origin, let $$P_{ij}\left( {x_{i},y_{j},f\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)} \right)$$ be the point on $$S$$ directly above it (see Figure 1). The tangent plane to $$S$$ at $$P_{ij}$$ is an approximation to $$S$$ near $$P_{ij}$$ . So the area $$\Delta T_{ij}$$ of the part of this tangent plane (a parallelogram) that lies directly above $$R_{ij}$$ is an approximation to the area $$\Delta S_{ij}$$ of the part of $$S$$ that lies directly above $$R_{ij}$$ . Thus the sum $$\Sigma{\Sigma{\Delta T_{ij}}}$$ is an approximation to the total area of $$S$$ , and this approximation appears to improve as the number of rectangles increases. Therefore we define the surface area of $$S$$ to be
$$A(S) = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\Delta T_{ij}}}$$

image.alt: Details A square, a curved surface, three shaded regions and eight line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The square, labeled D, lies on the x y plane with its top and left side parallel to the positive y and x axes, respectively. A curved surface, labeled S, resembling a square, bent concave down and parabolic sides is graphed directly above the square. A smaller square labeled R_(i j) is shaded within the larger square. The region within the square is labeled Delta A. A point marked at the back left corner of R_(i j) is labeled (x_i, y_j). Two parallel dashed line segments with a distance Delta x between them, begin from the positive x axis, run parallel to the positive y axis and meet R_(i j) at its back and front left corners. Two parallel dashed line segments with a distance Delta y between them, begin from the positive y axis, run parallel to the positive x axis and meet R_(i j) at its back left and right corners. Four vertical line segments rise upward from the four corners of R_(i j) and meet the curved surface. The curved square formed by the four points where the line segments meet the curved surface is shaded and labeled Delta S_(i j). A point is marked at the back left corner of the Delta S_(i j), directly above (x_i, y_j) and labeled P_(i j). Another small square plane, Delta T_(i j) is tangent to Delta S_(i j) at P_(i j).

section.paragraph: To find a formula that is more convenient than Equation 1 for computational purposes, we let $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ be the vectors that start at $$P_{ij}$$ and lie along the sides of the parallelogram with area $$\Delta T_{ij}$$ . (See Figure 2.) Then $$\Delta T_{ij} = \left| {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right|$$ . Recall from Section 14.3 that $$f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)$$ are the slopes of the tangent lines through $$P_{ij}$$ in the directions of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ . Therefore

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{a} = \Delta x\mathbf{i} + f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta x\mathbf{k}} \\ {\mathbf{b} = \Delta y\mathbf{j} + f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta y\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
and

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left| \begin{array}{llc} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {\Delta x} & 0 & {f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta x} \\ 0 & {\Delta y} & {f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta y} \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} = - f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta x\Delta y\mathbf{i} - f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\Delta x\Delta y\mathbf{j} + \Delta x\Delta y\mathbf{k}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} = \left\lbrack {- f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\mathbf{i} - f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}} \right\rbrack\Delta A} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details Two square regions, eight line segments, and two vectors are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. A square shaped region lies on the x y plane with its top and left side parallel to the positive y and x axes, respectively. Two parallel dashed line segments with a distance Delta x between them, begin from the positive x axis, run parallel to the positive y axis and meet the square region at its back and front left corners. Two parallel dashed line segments with a distance Delta y between them, begin from the positive y axis, run parallel to the positive x axis and meet the square at its back left and right corners. A slanted square region, labeled Delta T_(i j), lies directly above the square region in the x y plane. The side near the x z plane is elevated and the sides parallel to the y z plane slope down and to the right. Four vertical line segments rise upward from the four corners of R_(i j) and meet the corresponding corners of Delta T_(i j). A point is marked at the back left corner of the Delta T_(i j), and labeled P_(i j). A vector, labeled vector a, begins from P_(i j) and runs along the entire length of the left side of Delta T_(i j). Another vector, labeled vector b, begins from P_(i j) and runs along the entire length of the back side of Delta T_(i j).

section.paragraph: Thus
$$\Delta T_{ij} = \left| {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right| = \sqrt{{\lbrack{f_{x}{({x_{i},y_{j}})}}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{f_{y}{({x_{i},y_{j}})}}\rbrack}^{2} + 1}\Delta A$$
From Definition 1 we then have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A(S) = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\Delta T_{ij}}}} \\ {\phantom{A(S)} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\sqrt{\left\lbrack {f_{x}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {f_{y}\left( {x_{i},y_{j}} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2} + 1}\Delta A}}} \end{array}$$
and by the definition of a double integral we get the following formula.
The area of the surface with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right),\left( {x,y} \right) \in D$$ , where $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ are continuous, is
$$A(S) = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{\left\lbrack {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2} + 1}dA}}$$

We will verify in Section 16.6 that this formula is consistent with our previous formula for the area of a surface of revolution. If we use the alternative notation for partial derivatives, we can rewrite Formula 2 as follows:
$$A(S) = {\iint\limits_{D}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}}dA$$
Notice the similarity between the surface area formula in Equation 3 and the arc length formula from Section 8.1:
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}dx}}$$

example.paragraph: Using Formula 2 with $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + 2y + 2$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{T}{\sqrt{\left( {2x} \right)^{2} + (2)^{2} + 1}dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\sqrt{4x^{2} + 5}dydx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{0}^{1}{x\sqrt{4x^{2} + 5}}}dx = \frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{2}{3}\left. {({4x^{2} + 5})}^{3 \slash 2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{12}{({27 - 5\sqrt{5}})}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the area of the part of the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ that lies under the plane $$z = 9$$ .

Solution The plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ , $$z = 9$$ . Therefore the given surface lies above the disk $$D$$ with center the origin and radius $$3$$ . (See Figure 5.) Using Formula 3, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}}dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( {2x} \right)^{2} + \left( {2y} \right)^{2}}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + 4{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dA}}} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{3}{\sqrt{1 + 4r^{2}}rdrd\theta =}}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{3}{\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{1 + 4r^{2}}\left( {8r} \right)dr}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. {2\pi{\left( \frac{1}{8} \right)}\frac{2}{3}{({1 + 4r^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{\pi}{6}{({37\sqrt{37} - 1})}} \end{array}$$

The back left and front right corners bend upward, with the square bending concave up along the diagonal. A circular region in the middle of the square is shaded. It shares its center with the square. A shaded circular region labeled D and described by x^2 + y^2 <= 1, z = 0 lies on the x y plane, directly below the circular region on the curved surface, with its center at the origin.

If you attempt to use Formula 2 to find the area of the top half of the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = a^{2}$$ , you have a slight problem because the double integral is improper. In fact, the integrand has an infinite discontinuity at every point of the boundary circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ . However, the integral can be computed as the limit of the integral over the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant t^{2}$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow a^{-} \right.$$ . Use this method to show that the area of a sphere of radius $$a$$ is $$4\pi a^{2}$$ .

section.heading: 15.6. Triple Integrals
section.paragraph: Just as we defined single integrals for functions of one variable and double integrals for functions of two variables, so we can define triple integrals for functions of three variables.
section.heading: Triple Integrals over Rectangular Boxes
section.paragraph: Let’s first deal with the simplest case where $$f$$ is defined on a rectangular box:
$$B = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|}a \leqslant x \leqslant b,c \leqslant y \leqslant d,r \leqslant z \leqslant s \right\}$$

The first step is to divide $$B$$ into sub-boxes. We do this by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$l$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta x$$ , dividing $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ into $$m$$ subintervals of width $$\Delta y$$ , and dividing $$\left\lbrack {r,s} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of width $$\Delta z$$ . The planes through the endpoints of these subintervals parallel to the coordinate planes divide the box $$B$$ into $$lmn$$ sub-boxes
$$B_{\mathit{ijk}} = {\lbrack{x_{i - 1},x_{i}}\rbrack} \times {\lbrack{y_{j - 1},y_{j}}\rbrack} \times {\lbrack{z_{k - 1},z_{k}}\rbrack}$$
which are shown in Figure 1. Each sub-box has volume $$\Delta V = \Delta x\Delta y\Delta z$$ .

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. In both parts, a rectangular box is graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. In the first part, the box is labeled B and is divided into tiny cubes of equal size. In the second part, the outline of the box and a single tiny cube is displayed. An enlarged view of the cube shows the cube to be labeled B_(i j k). The sides of the cube parallel to the x, y, and z axes are labeled Delta x, Delta y, and Delta z, respectively.

section.paragraph: Then we form the triple Riemann sum
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{f{({x_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},y_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},z_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*}})}\Delta V}}}$$

where the sample point $$({x_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast},y_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast},z_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast}})$$ is in $$B_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ . By analogy with the definition of a double integral (15.1.5), we define the triple integral as the limit of the triple Riemann sums in (2).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The triple integral of $$f$$ over the box $$B$$ is

$${\iiint\limits_{B}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV} = \lim\limits_{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}f}}{({x_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},y_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},z_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*}})}\Delta V$$
if this limit exists.

section.paragraph: Again, the triple integral always exists if $$f$$ is continuous. We can choose the sample point to be any point in the sub-box, but if we choose it to be the point $$\left( {x_{i},y_{j},z_{k}} \right)$$ we get a simpler-looking expression for the triple integral:

$${\iiint\limits_{B}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = \lim\limits_{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}f}}{({x_{i},y_{j},z_{k}})}\Delta V$$
Just as for double integrals, the practical method for evaluating triple integrals is to express them as iterated integrals as follows.

note.title: Fubini’s Theorem for Triple Integrals
note.heading: Fubini’s Theorem for Triple Integrals
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on the rectangular box $$B = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {r,s} \right\rbrack$$ , then
$${\iiint\limits_{B}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{r}^{s}{\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{a}^{b}f}}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz}$$

section.paragraph: The iterated integral on the right side of Fubini’s Theorem means that we integrate first with respect to $$x$$ (keeping $$y$$ and $$z$$ fixed), then we integrate with respect to $$y$$ (keeping $$z$$ fixed), and finally we integrate with respect to $$z$$ . There are five other possible orders in which we can integrate, all of which give the same value. For instance, if we integrate with respect to $$y$$ , then $$z$$ , and then $$x$$ , we have
$${\iiint\limits_{B}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{r}^{s}{\int_{c}^{d}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate the triple integral $${\iiint_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$B$$ is the rectangular box given by
$$B = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1, - 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 3 \right\}$$
Solution We could use any of the six possible orders of integration. If we choose to integrate with respect to $$x$$ , then $$y$$ , and then $$z$$ , we obtain

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{xyz^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz} =}}}}{\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}yz^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 1}}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}{\int_{- 1}^{2}{\frac{yz^{2}}{2}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dz} =}}}{\int_{0}^{3}{\left\lbrack \frac{y^{2}z^{2}}{4} \right\rbrack_{y = - 1}^{y = 2}\mathit{dz}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}{xyz^{2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{3}\frac{3z^{2}}{4}}\mathit{dz} = \left. \frac{z^{3}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \frac{27}{4}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Triple Integrals over General Regions
section.paragraph: Now we define the triple integral over a general bounded region $$\mathbf{E}$$ in three-dimensional space (a solid) by much the same procedure that we used for double integrals (15.2.2). We enclose $$E$$ in a box $$B$$ of the type given by Equation 1. Then we define $$F$$ so that it agrees with $$f$$ on $$E$$ but is $$0$$ for points in $$B$$ that are outside $$E$$ . By definition,
$${\iiint\limits_{E}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}}\mathit{dV} = {\iiint\limits_{B}{F{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}}}$$

This integral exists if $$f$$ is continuous and the boundary of $$E$$ is “reasonably smooth.” The triple integral has essentially the same properties as the double integral (Properties 5, 6, 7, and 8 in Section 15.2).

We restrict our attention to continuous functions $$f$$ and to certain simple types of regions. A solid region $$E$$ is said to be of type 1 if it lies between the graphs of two continuous functions of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , that is,
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)\left. \middle| \left( {x,y} \right) \right. \in D,u_{1}{\left( {x,y} \right)} \leqslant z \leqslant u_{2}{\left( {x,y} \right)}} \right\}$$

where $$D$$ is the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane as shown in Figure 2. Notice that the upper boundary of the solid $$E$$ is the surface with equation $$z = u_{2}{\left( {x,y} \right)}$$ , while the lower boundary is the surface $$z = u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

image.alt: Details An irregular solid, a shaded region, and three line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, resembles an irregular cylinder. It has a base, labeled z = u_1(x, y), and a top side, labeled z = u_2(x, y), and a curved side that connects the top and the base. The projection of the solid is a shaded area labeled D, lying on the x y plane. Three vertical dashed line segments from E descend downward to meet the x y plane at the extreme points of D.

section.paragraph: By the same sort of argument that led to (15.2.3), it can be shown that if $$E$$ is a type 1 region given by Equation 5, then
$${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {{\int_{u_{1}{({x,y})}}^{u_{2}{({x,y})}}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}\mathit{dz}} \right\rbrack}\mathit{dA}$$

The meaning of the inner integral on the right side of Equation 6 is that $$x$$ and $$y$$ are held fixed, and therefore $$u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ are regarded as constants, while $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is integrated with respect to $$z$$ .
In particular, if the projection $$D$$ of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is a type I plane region (as in Figure 3), then
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|a \leqslant x \leqslant b,g_{1}(x) \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}(x),u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right) \leqslant z \leqslant u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\}$$
and Equation 6 becomes
$${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{g_{1}{(x)}}^{g_{2}{(x)}}{\int_{u_{1}{({x,y})}}^{u_{2}{({x,y})}}f}}}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}$$
If, on the other hand, $$D$$ is a type II plane region (as in Figure 4), then
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|c \leqslant y \leqslant d,h_{1}(y) \leqslant x \leqslant h_{2}(y),u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right) \leqslant z \leqslant u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\}$$
and Equation 6 becomes
$${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{h_{1}{(y)}}^{h_{2}{(y)}}{\int_{u_{1}{({x,y})}}^{u_{2}{({x,y})}}{f{({x,y,z})}}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}$$

There are two tick marks on the positive x axis: a and b, with a lying between the origin and b. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, resembles an irregular cylinder. It has a base, labeled z = u_1(x, y), and a top side, labeled z = u_2(x, y), and a curved side that connects the top and the base. The base and the top side resemble irregular sectors. The projection of the solid is a shaded area labeled D, lying on the x y plane. D resembles a trapezium with curved sides. The longer side is near and parallel to the positive y axis and in line with the tick mark a. The shorter side is parallel to the positive y axis and in line with the tick mark b. The left slanted side of D is labeled y = g_1(x) and the right slanted side is labeled y = g_2(x). Four vertical dashed line segments from E descend downward to meet the x y plane at the extreme points of D.

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. There are two tick marks on the positive y axis: c and d, with c lying between the origin and d. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}$$ , where $$E$$ is the solid in the first octant bounded by the surface $$z = 12xy$$ and the planes $$y = x$$ , $$x = 1$$ .

Solution When we set up a triple integral it’s wise to draw two diagrams: one of the solid region $$E$$ (Figure 5) and, for a type 1 region, one of its projection $$D$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane (Figure 6). The lower boundary of the solid $$E$$ is the plane $$z = 0$$ and the upper boundary is the surface $$z = 12xy$$ , so we use $$u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ and $$u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right) = 12xy$$ in Formula 7. Notice that the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane is the triangular region shown in Figure 6, and we have
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 12xy} \right\}$$

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the right. The positive y axis slopes up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, has a triangular base on the x y plane with one of its sides along the x axis between x = 0 and x = 1. The right side of the solid is a right triangle with a linear hypotenuse. The left side of the solid is a right triangle with a concave up hypotenuse. The top surface of the solid is labeled z = 12 x y and completes the solid.

Details A triangle, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The triangle is a right triangle with its vertices at (1, 1), (1,0), and (0, 0). The hypotenuse of the triangle is labeled y = x. The region within the triangle is shaded and labeled D. A vertical line segment is drawn from the bottom side to the hypotenuse and an arrow head placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: This description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region enables us to evaluate the integral as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\int_{0}^{12xy}{z\mathit{dz}}}}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}\left\lbrack \frac{z^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack}}_{z = 0}^{z = 12xy}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{\left( {12xy} \right)^{2}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = 72}}}{\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x}x^{2}y^{2}}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{z\mathit{dV}}} = {72{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {x^{2}\frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = x}\mathit{dx}} = 24\int_{0}^{1}x^{5}\mathit{dx} = 24\left\lbrack \frac{x^{6}}{6} \right\rbrack_{x = 0}^{x = 1} = 4}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Figure 7 shows how the solid $$E$$ of Example 2 is swept out by the iterated triple integral if we integrate first with respect to $$z$$ , then $$y$$ , then $$x$$ .

The positive y axis slopes up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid has a triangular base on the x y plane with one of its sides along the x axis between x = 0 and x = 1. The right side of the solid is a right triangle with a linear hypotenuse. The left side of the solid is a right triangle with a concave up hypotenuse. The top surface completes the solid. In the first part, two points, and a line segment with an arrowhead is drawn within the solid. The first point is on the base of the solid, on the x y plane. The second point is directly above the first point, on the top surface. A vertical line segment connects both the points. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points upward. In the second part, a vertical cross section of the solid, parallel to the y z plane, is highlighted. A vertical line segment is drawn on the cross section, from the base to the top side, parallel to the z axis. Another small arrow is drawn perpendicular to the line segment, at approximately its middle, pointing backward. In the third part, four vertical cross sections, approximately equally spaced, parallel to the x z plane are highlighted. A small horizontal arrow is placed on each of the cross sections, at approximately the middle, all of them pointing toward the right side of the solid.

section.paragraph: A solid region $$E$$ is of type 2 if it is of the form
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|\left( {y,z} \right) \in D,u_{1}\left( {y,z} \right) \leqslant x \leqslant u_{2}\left( {y,z} \right)} \right\}$$

where, this time, $$D$$ is the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane (see Figure 8). The back surface is $$x = u_{1}\left( {y,z} \right)$$ , the front surface is $$x = u_{2}\left( {y,z} \right)$$ , and we have
$${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left\lbrack {{\int_{u_{1}{({y,z})}}^{u_{2}{({y,z})}}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dx}} \right\rbrack\mathit{dA}}}$$

image.alt: Details An irregular solid, a shaded region, and two line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, resembles an irregular cylinder flattened along its length. It has a back face, labeled z = u_1(x, y), and a front, labeled z = u_2(x, y), and a curved side that connects the front and back sides. The front and back sides resemble the sole of a shoe and the length of the cylinder is parallel to the x y plane. The projection of the back face is shaded on the y z plane and labeled D. Two horizontal dashed line segments from the left and right extremes of the back face of E run parallel to the x y plane to meet the left and right extreme points of D, respectively.

section.paragraph: Finally, a type 3 region is of the form
$$E = \left\{ {{({x,y,z})}|{({x,z})} \in D,u_{1}{({x,z})} \leqslant y \leqslant u_{2}{({x,z})}} \right\}$$

where $$D$$ is the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, $$y = u_{1}\left( {x,z} \right)$$ is the left surface, and $$y = u_{2}\left( {x,z} \right)$$ is the right surface (see Figure 9). For this type of region we have
$${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left\lbrack {{\int_{u_{1}{({x,z})}}^{u_{2}{({x,z})}}f}{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dy}} \right\rbrack\mathit{dA}}}$$

image.alt: Details An irregular solid, a shaded region, and two line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, resembles an irregular cylinder. Its axis is parallel to the x y plane and y z plane. The left and right faces of the cylinder resemble curved ellipses. The projection of the left face is shaded on the x z plane. It almost resembles an ellipse and is labeled D. Two horizontal dashed line segments from the top and bottom extremes of the left face of E run parallel to the x y plane and y z plane to meet the top and bottom extreme points of D, respectively.

section.paragraph: In each of Equations 10 and 11 there may be two possible expressions for the integral depending on whether $$D$$ is a type I or type II plane region (and corresponding to Equations 7 and 8).

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}$$ , where $$E$$ is the region bounded by the paraboloid $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and the plane $$y = 4$$ .

Solution The solid $$E$$ is shown in Figure 10. If we regard it as a type 1 region, then we need to consider its projection $$D_{1}$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, which is the parabolic region shown in Figures 10 and 11. (The trace of $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ in the plane $$z = 0$$ is the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ .)

The positive y axis slopes up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The paraboloid, labeled E and defined by y = x^2 + z^2 has its vertex at the origin, and opens along the positive y axis until y = 4. A horizontal cross section of the paraboloid is shaded. It lies on the x y plane and is a parabolic region labeled D_1 with its vertex at the origin and opening along the positive y axis. A vertical trace parallel to the x z plane is drawn on the surface of the paraboloid. It is a circle with its center on the positive y axis.

Details A parabola and a line are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The parabola, labeled y = x^2, opens upward with its vertex at the origin. The line is horizontal, labeled y = 4, runs parallel to the x axis crossing both the arms of the parabola. The region bound by the parabola and the line is shaded and labeled D_1.

example.paragraph: From $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ we obtain $$z = \pm \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ , so the lower boundary surface of $$E$$ is $$z = - \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ and the upper surface is $$z = \sqrt{y - x^{2}}$$ . Therefore the description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region is
$$E = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| - 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2,x^{2} \leqslant y \leqslant 4, - \sqrt{y - x^{2}} \leqslant z \leqslant \sqrt{y - x^{2}} \right\}$$
and so we obtain
$${\iiint\limits_{E}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{- 2}^{2}{\int_{x^{2}}^{4}{\int_{- \sqrt{y - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{y - x^{2}}}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$

Although this expression is correct, it is extremely difficult to evaluate. So let’s instead consider $$E$$ as a region of a different type. If we regard $$E$$ as a type 3 region, then we need to consider its projection $$D_{3}$$ onto the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, which is the disk $$x^{2} + z^{2} \leqslant 4$$ shown in Figures 12 and 13. (The trace of $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ in the plane $$y = 4$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ .)

The positive y axis slopes up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The paraboloid, labeled E, has its vertex at the origin, and opens along the positive y axis until y = 4. A circular shaded region labeled D_3 lies on the x z plane with its center at the origin. A vertical trace parallel to the x z plane is drawn on the surface of the paraboloid. It is a circle with its center on the positive y axis.

example.paragraph: Then the left boundary of $$E$$ is the paraboloid $$y = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and the right boundary is the plane $$y = 4$$ , so taking $$u_{1}\left( {x,z} \right) = x^{2} + z^{2}$$ and $$u_{2}\left( {x,z} \right) = 4$$ in Equation 11, we have

$${\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV} =}}{\iint\limits_{D_{3}}\left\lbrack {\int_{x^{2} + z^{2}}^{4}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dy}}} \right\rbrack}\mathit{dA} = {\iint\limits_{D_{3}}{({4 - x^{2} - z^{2}})}}\sqrt{x^{2} - z^{2}}\mathit{dA}$$
Although this integral could be written as
it’s easier to convert to polar coordinates in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$z = r\sin\theta$$ . This gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}} = {\iint\limits_{D_{3}}{{({4 - x^{2} - z^{2}})}\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{2}{{({4 - r^{2}})}rr\mathit{dr}d\theta =}}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{2}{{({4r^{2} - r^{4}})}\mathit{dr}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}{\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}\mathit{dV}}} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{4r^{3}}{3} - \frac{r^{5}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{128\pi}{15}}} \end{array}$$

The most difficult step in evaluating a triple integral is setting up an expression for the region of integration (such as Equation 9 in Example 2). Remember that the limits of integration in the inner integral contain at most two variables, the limits of integration in the middle integral contain at most one variable, and the limits of integration in the outer integral must be constants.

section.heading: Changing the Order of Integration
section.paragraph: Fubini’s Theorem for Triple Integrals allows us to express a triple integral as an iterated integral, and there are six different orders of integration in which we can do this. Given an iterated integral, it may be advantageous to change the order of integration because evaluating an iterated integral in one order may be simpler than in another. In the next example we investigate equivalent iterated integrals using different orders of integration.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Express the iterated integral $${\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x^{2}}{\int_{0}^{y}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$ as a triple integral and then rewrite it as an iterated integral in the following orders.

list.item: (a) Integrate first with respect to $$x$$ , then $$z$$ , and then $$y$$ .
(b) Integrate first with respect to $$y$$ , then $$x$$ , and then $$z$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution We can write
$${\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x^{2}}{\int_{0}^{y}f}}}\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = {\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$

where $$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2},0 \leqslant z \leqslant y} \right\}$$ . From this description of $$E$$ as a type 1 region we see that $$E$$ lies between the lower surface $$z = 0$$ and the upper surface $$z = y$$ , and its projection onto the $$xy$$ -plane is $$\left\{ {\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}} \right\}$$ , as shown in Figures 14 and 15. So $$E$$ is the solid enclosed by the planes $$z = 0$$ , $$x = 1$$ , $$y = z$$ and the parabolic cylinder $$y = x^{2}$$ (or $$x = \sqrt{y}$$ ).

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the right. The positive y axis slopes up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, has a triangular base on the x y plane. The triangular base is a right triangle with one side along the x axis between x = 0 and x = 1, one side parallel to the y axis between (1, 0) and (1, 1) and a curved hypotenuse that traces a parabolic path, defined by y = x^2, from the origin until (1, 1). The right side of the solid is a right triangle with a linear hypotenuse and is labeled x = 1. The left side of the solid is a portion of a paraboloid with its vertex at the origin and opening along the positive y axis from the origin until y = 1. The top surface of the solid is labeled z = y and completes the solid.

Details The figure has three parts. In the first part a shaded region labeled D_1 is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The region is a right triangle with two linear sides and a curved hypotenuse. The base lies on the x axis between the origin and (1, 0). The right side is vertical and runs parallel to the y axis from (1, 0) to (1, 1). The third side traces a parabola defined by y = x^2 from the origin until (1, 1). In the second part a shaded region labeled D_2 is graphed in the first quadrant of the y z coordinate plane. The positive y axis is horizontal while the positive z axis is vertical. The region is a right triangle with its vertices at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (1, 1). The hypotenuse is labeled z =y. In the third part a shaded region labeled D_3 is graphed in the x z coordinate plane. The positive x axis is horizontal while the positive z axis is vertical. The region is a right triangle with two linear sides and a curved hypotenuse. The base lies on the x axis between the origin and (1, 0). The right side is vertical and runs parallel to the z axis from (1, 0) to (1, 1). The third side traces a parabola defined by z = x^2 from the origin until (1, 1).

example.paragraph: Using Figure 14 as a guide, we can write projections onto the three coordinate planes as follows (see Figure 15):

$$\begin{array}{lll} {{onto the}\mathit{xy}{-plane}: D_{1}} & = & {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {x,y} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,\sqrt{y} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}} \\ {{onto the}\mathit{yz}{-plane}: D_{2}} & = & {\{{\left( {y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant y}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,z \leqslant y \leqslant 1}\}} \\ {{onto the}\mathit{xz}{-plane}: D_{3}} & = & {\{{\left( {x,z} \right)|0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant x^{2}}\}} \\ & = & {\{{\left( {x,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,\sqrt{z} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}} \end{array}$$

list.item: (a) In order to integrate first with respect to $$x$$ , then $$z$$ , and then $$y$$ , we need to consider $$E$$ as a type 2 region where the back boundary is the surface $$x = \sqrt{y}$$ and the front boundary is the plane $$x = 1$$ ; the projection onto the $$yz$$ -plane is $$D_{2}$$ . We describe $$E$$ by $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant y,\sqrt{y} \leqslant x \leqslant 1}\}}$$ and then $${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{y}{\int_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}f}}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}$$

(b) In order to integrate first with respect to $$y$$ , then $$x$$ , and then $$z$$ , we need to consider $$E$$ as a type 3 region where the left boundary is the plane $$y = z$$ and the right boundary is the surface $$y = x^{2}$$ . The projection onto the $$xz$$ -plane is $$D_{3}$$ and $$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)|0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1,\sqrt{z} \leqslant x \leqslant 1,z \leqslant y \leqslant x^{2}}\}}$$ and then $${\iiint\limits_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int_{z}^{x^{2}}f}}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dz}$$

section.heading: Applications of Triple Integrals
section.paragraph: Recall that if $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ , then the single integral $${\int_{a}^{b}f}{(x)}\mathit{dx}$$ represents the area under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ , and if $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , then the double integral $${\iint_{D}f}\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}$$ represents the volume under the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and above $$D$$ . The corresponding interpretation of a triple integral $${\iiint_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , is not very useful because it would be the “hypervolume” of a four-dimensional object and, of course, that is very difficult to visualize. (Remember that $$E$$ is just the domain of the function $$f$$ ; the graph of $$f$$ lies in four-dimensional space.) Nonetheless, the triple integral $${\iiint_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$ can be interpreted in different ways in different physical situations, depending on the physical interpretations of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , $$z$$ , and $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ .
Let’s begin with the special case where $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ for all points in $$E$$ . Then the triple integral does represent the volume of $$E$$ :
$$V(E) = {\iiint\limits_{E}\mathit{dV}}$$
For example, you can see this in the case of a type 1 region by putting $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ in Formula 6:

$${\iiint\limits_{E}{1\mathit{dV}}} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\int_{u_{1}{({x,y})}}^{u_{2}{({x,y})}}\mathit{dz}} \right\rbrack}\mathit{dA} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {u_{2}{({x,y})} - u_{1}{({x,y})}} \right\rbrack}\mathit{dA}$$
and from Section 15.2 we know this represents the volume that lies between the surfaces $$z = u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$z = u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Use a triple integral to find the volume of the tetrahedron $$T$$ bounded by the planes $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , $$x = 2y$$ , $$x = 0$$ , and $$z = 0$$ .

Solution The tetrahedron $$T$$ and its projection $$D$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane are shown in Figures 16 and 17. The lower boundary of $$T$$ is the plane $$z = 0$$ and the upper boundary is the plane $$x + 2y + z = 2$$ , that is, $$z = 2 - x - 2y$$ .

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a tetrahedron is graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The tetrahedron is labeled T and its base lies on the first quadrant of the x y plane with its vertices at the origin and the points labeled (0, 1, 0) and (1, 1/2, 0). The top vertex of the tetrahedron is at the point labeled (0, 0, 2). The left face of the tetrahedron is labeled x = 2 y and the right face is labeled x + 2 y + z = 2. The back face is on the y z plane.

Details A triangular region and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes have a single tick mark labeled 1. The triangular region has its vertices at (0, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1/2) and is labeled D. The left side of the region is along the positive y axis. The top side, which slopes downward to the right from (0. 1) to (1, 1/2) is labeled x + 2 y = 2 or y = 1 minus x/2. The bottom side, which slopes upward to the right from the origin to (1, 1/2) is labeled y = x/2. A vertical line segment is drawn from the bottom side to the top side. An arrowhead placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: Therefore we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {V(T) = {\iiint\limits_{T}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x/2}^{1 - x/2}{\int_{0}^{2 - x - 2y}{dzdydx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V(T)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x \slash 2}^{1 - x \slash 2}{\left( {2 - x - 2y} \right)\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{3}}}}} \end{array}$$
by the same calculation as in Example 15.2.4.
(Notice that it is not necessary to use triple integrals to compute volumes. They simply give an alternative method for setting up the calculation.)

section.paragraph: All the applications of double integrals in Section 15.4 can be extended to triple integrals using analogous reasoning. For example, suppose that a solid object occupying a region $$E$$ has density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ , in units of mass per unit volume, at each point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in $$E$$ . To find the total mass $$m$$ of $$E$$ we divide a rectangular box $$B$$ containing $$E$$ into subboxes $$B_{ijk}$$ of the same size (as in Figure 18), and consider $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ to be $$0$$ outside $$E$$ . If we choose a point $${({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V$$ in $$B_{ijk}$$ , then the mass of the part of $$E$$ that occupies $$B_{ijk}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V$$ , where $$\Delta V$$ is the volume of $$B_{ijk}$$ . We get an approximation to the total mass by adding the (approximate) masses of all the sub-boxes, and if we increase the number of sub-boxes, we obtain the total mass $$m$$ of $$E$$ as the limiting value of the approximations:

$$m = \lim\limits_{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{\rho{({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V =}}{\iiint\limits_{E}\rho}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$

image.alt: Details A solid and a cuboid are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. In the first part, the cuboid, labeled B, is divided into tiny cubes of equal size. A solid, labeled E, resembling an ellipsoid is shaded within the cuboid. One of the cubes inside the ellipsoid is shaded with a different color. An enlarged view shows the shaded cube labeled B_(i j k). A point within the cube is labeled (x^*_(i j k), y^*_(i j k),,z^*_(i j k)).

figure.caption: The mass of each sub-box $$B_{ijk}$$ is approximated by $${\rho({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V$$

section.paragraph: Similarly, the moments of $$E$$ about the three coordinate planes are

$$\begin{matrix} {M_{\mathit{yz}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{x\rho}}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} M_{\mathit{xz}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}y}\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}} \\ {M_{\mathit{xy}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}z}\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}} \end{matrix}$$
The center of mass is located at the point $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y},\overline{z}} \right)$$ , where
$${\overline{x} = \frac{M_{\mathit{yz}}}{m}} {\overline{y} = \frac{M_{\mathit{xz}}}{m}} {\overline{z} = \frac{M_{\mathit{xy}}}{m}}$$
If the density is constant, the center of mass of the solid is called the centroid of $$E$$ . The moments of inertia about the three coordinate axes are
As in Section 15.4, the total electric charge on a solid object occupying a region $$E$$ and having charge density $$\sigma\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is
$$Q = {\iiint\limits_{E}\sigma}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$

If we have three continuous random variables $$X$$ , $$Y$$ , and $$Z$$ , their joint density function is a function of three variables such that the probability that $$\left( {X,Y,Z} \right)$$ lies in $$E$$ is
$$P\left( {\left( {X,Y,Z} \right) \in E} \right) = {\iiint\limits_{E}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}\mathit{dV}$$
In particular,
$$P\left( {a \leqslant X \leqslant b,c \leqslant Y \leqslant d,r \leqslant Z \leqslant s} \right) = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{r}^{s}\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx}$$
The joint density function satisfies
$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) \geqslant 0 {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}}}\mathit{dz}\mathit{dy}\mathit{dx} = 1$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find the center of mass of a solid of constant density that is bounded by the parabolic cylinder $$x = y^{2}$$ and the planes $$x = z$$ , $$z = 0$$ , and $$x = 1$$ .

Solution The solid $$E$$ and its projection onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane are shown in Figure 19. The lower and upper surfaces of $$E$$ are the planes $$z = 0$$ and $$z = x$$ , so we describe $$E$$ as a type 1 region:
$$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right){|{- 1 \leqslant y \leqslant 1,y^{2} \leqslant x \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant z \leqslant x}}}\}}$$
Then, if the density is $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \rho$$ , the mass is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iiint\limits_{E}{\rho\mathit{dV} = \int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{y^{2}}^{1}\int_{0}^{x}\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = \rho\int_{- 1}^{1}\int_{y^{2}}^{1}x\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack}_{x = y^{2}}^{x = 1}\mathit{dy}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\frac{\rho}{2}{\int_{- 1}^{1}{({1 - y^{4}})}}\mathit{dy} = \rho{\int_{0}^{1}{({1 - y^{4}})}}\mathit{dy}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\rho\left\lbrack {y - \frac{y^{5}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4\rho}{5}}} \end{array}$$

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, has five sides. The top and bottom sides are parabolic regions. The bottom side lies on the x y plane, has its vertex at the origin and opens along the positive x axis until x = 1. The top side, labeled z = x, has its vertex at the origin, opens up and to the left, directly above the bottom side. The front side is rectangular and parallel to the y z plane. The left and right sides are curved triangular regions that complete the solid. In the second part, a parabola, a line, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrow head are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The parabola, labeled x = y^2, opens rightward, is symmetric about the x axis, and has its vertex at the origin. The line, labeled x = 1, is vertical and runs parallel to the y axis, to its right. The region bound by the parabola and the line is shaded and labeled D. The line segment is horizontal, runs rightward and connects the parabola to the line in the fourth quadrant. The arrowhead placed on the line points rightward.

example.paragraph: Because of the symmetry of $$E$$ and $$\rho$$ about the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane, we can immediately say that $$M_{\mathit{xz}} = 0$$ and therefore $$\overline{y} = 0$$ . The other moments are

$$\begin{array}{l} {M_{\mathit{yz}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{x\rho\mathit{dV}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{x\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{yz}}} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{x^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} = \rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\left\lbrack \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{x = y^{2}}^{x = 1}\mathit{dy}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{yz}}} = {\frac{2\rho}{3}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({1 - y^{6}})}\mathit{dy}}} = \frac{2\rho}{3}\left\lbrack {y - \frac{y^{7}}{7}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4\rho}{7}}} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {M_{\mathit{xy}} = {\iiint\limits_{E}{z\rho\mathit{dV}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\int_{0}^{x}{z\rho\mathit{dz}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{xy}}} = {\rho{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{\left\lbrack \frac{z^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{z = 0}^{z = x}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}} = \frac{\rho}{2}{\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{y^{2}}^{1}{x^{2}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{M_{\mathit{xy}}} = {\frac{\rho}{3}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({1 - y^{6}})}\mathit{dy} = \frac{2\rho}{7}}}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the center of mass is

$$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y},\overline{z}} \right) = \left( {\frac{M_{\mathit{yz}}}{m},\frac{M_{\mathit{xz}}}{m},\frac{M_{\mathit{xy}}}{m}} \right) = \left( {\frac{5}{7},0,\frac{5}{14}} \right)$$
